lessons.title: Europe in 1894: Empires, Alliances and the Long Fuse
lessons.description: Five Great Powers, Bismarck's diplomacy, and the 1894 alliance that ended French isolation.
lessons.content_html:
Europe in 1894: Five Great Powers

In 1894 the European continent was dominated by five so-called Great Powers: Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia. Each had a different mix of strengths and worries. Britain had the largest empire and the world’s strongest navy, but a small regular army. France had a powerful army and overseas empire, but had not forgotten losing Alsace-Lorraine to Germany in 1871. Germany was the youngest of the powers, unified only in 1871, but its industry was the fastest-growing in Europe. Austria-Hungary was a multi-ethnic empire of Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles and Slavs — held together with difficulty. Russia was vast, populous and rich in resources, but technologically behind and politically unstable.

Key Fact

By 1894 the five European Great Powers — Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia — each pursued a distinct interest: empire and naval supremacy, recovery of Alsace-Lorraine, industrial expansion, holding the multi-ethnic empire together, and access to the Mediterranean.

Bismarck’s System: Keep France Isolated

After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, Germany’s first chancellor Otto von Bismarck built his foreign policy around one fixed idea: France must never find an ally. A bitter France would always want Alsace-Lorraine back, so Bismarck made sure France stood alone in Europe. He achieved this through a web of treaties. The Three Emperors’ League of 1873 tied Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia together. The Dual Alliance of 1879 then bound Germany and Austria-Hungary in a defensive pact. In 1882 Italy joined to form the Triple Alliance. Even when Russia drifted away from the Three Emperors’ League over Balkan rivalries with Austria-Hungary, Bismarck kept Russia close with the secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887.

Bismarck believed Germany should be a satisfied, status-quo power. Having defeated France and unified Germany, he wanted no more wars. He worried about a ‘nightmare of coalitions’ — a future where France found powerful allies and Germany faced a war on two fronts. To prevent that, he kept Germany’s ambitions in Europe modest and avoided major colonial adventures, even though many Germans wanted an empire to match Britain’s. His message to the Reichstag in 1888 was blunt: ‘We Germans fear God, but nothing else in the world.’ Yet his diplomacy showed plenty of caution underneath the bravado.

Wilhelm II Dismisses Bismarck

Bismarck’s system depended on him personally managing it. In 1888 the new emperor Kaiser Wilhelm II came to the throne — young, impulsive and determined to be his own chancellor. In March 1890 he forced Bismarck to resign. The dismissal was famously caricatured in the British magazine Punch as ‘Dropping the Pilot’: an anxious old seaman climbing down the ship’s ladder while the young Kaiser leaned over the rail. Within months Wilhelm allowed the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to lapse, judging it incompatible with Germany’s alliance with Austria-Hungary. He underestimated the consequences. Russia, suddenly without a German guarantee, looked elsewhere for security.

The Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894

France saw its opportunity. The Third Republic was a parliamentary democracy; Russia was an autocratic monarchy under Tsar Alexander III — an unlikely match. Yet shared interest in containing Germany pulled them together. From 1891 French capital began funding Russian railway and industrial projects. In August 1892 secret military talks produced a draft military convention; in January 1894 it was formally ratified by the Tsar and the French president. The Franco-Russian Alliance bound each side to mobilise if the other was attacked by Germany, or by Austria-Hungary or Italy if those were backed by Germany.

For France, this was the diplomatic breakthrough Bismarck had spent two decades preventing. France was no longer alone. For Germany, the nightmare of a two-front war became a real strategic problem. German planners now had to imagine a war fought simultaneously in the west against France and in the east against Russia — the puzzle the Schlieffen Plan would later try to solve.

In 1894 Britain stood deliberately apart from European alliances. This policy was nicknamed Splendid Isolation. The phrase was coined by Canadian politician George Foster in 1896 and quickly adopted in London. Britain relied on the Royal Navy to protect its empire and trade routes, and saw little need to be tied to European quarrels. Yet by 1894 the policy was beginning to look strained: rivalries with France over Africa and with Russia over Persia and Afghanistan made permanent isolation harder to sustain.

The Long Fuse

Historians often call 1894 the start of the slow collapse of Bismarck’s European balance. The Franco-Russian Alliance did not cause war — it was a defensive pact and twenty years of peace would still follow. But it changed the geometry of Europe. Germany now faced a two-front problem; France had a powerful eastern partner; Britain’s isolation began to feel less splendid. Christopher Clark’s study The Sleepwalkers argues that none of the European powers wanted a continental war, but the alliance commitments they accumulated in this period made one increasingly possible. The fuse was now in place; the spark would come twenty years later, in Sarajevo.

Key Fact

The Franco-Russian Alliance was formally ratified in January 1894. It ended Bismarck’s policy of French isolation and forced German planners to prepare for a two-front war — the strategic problem the Schlieffen Plan would later try to solve.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Source Analysis question on this topic, you need to identify two reasons or features clearly from the source itself, not just describe what it says. Quote a short phrase to anchor each point. Watch out for sources that mix opinion with fact — the examiner wants you to read carefully and pick out the specific reason given, not pad your answer with own knowledge that the source does not support.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Europe in 1894 was dominated by five Great Powers, each with distinct interests — Britain’s navy and empire, France’s recovery of Alsace-Lorraine, Germany’s industrial rise, Austria-Hungary’s ethnic strains and Russia’s vast resources.
  • Bismarck’s diplomatic system kept France isolated through the Triple Alliance and the Reinsurance Treaty — a system Wilhelm II dismantled by sacking Bismarck and dropping Russia in 1890.
  • The Franco-Russian Alliance of January 1894 ended French isolation and gave Germany the two-front strategic problem that would shape every subsequent crisis.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by French foreign minister Théophile Delcassé to the French Chamber of Deputies, March 1895, drawn from the archives of the French Foreign Ministry.
‘For two decades since the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, France has stood alone. The new accord with Russia changes this. Our eastern partner doubles every soldier France can put in the field, and the German general staff in Berlin must now reckon with a war on two fronts whenever it considers war on one.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Delcassé gives for the importance of the Franco-Russian Alliance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• The alliance ended twenty years of French isolation following the loss of Alsace-Lorraine.
• Russia doubles France’s effective military strength (‘doubles every soldier France can put in the field’).
• Germany must now plan for a two-front war (‘a war on two fronts whenever it considers war on one’).

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Bismarck’s diplomatic system unravelled between 1888 and 1894.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Wilhelm II accession, Bismarck dismissal, lapse of Reinsurance Treaty, French loans to Russia, Franco-Russian Alliance); reaches the 1894 alliance through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1888: Wilhelm II inherited the German throne, determined to be his own chancellor.
• March 1890: Wilhelm dismissed Bismarck (‘Dropping the Pilot’).
• 1890: Wilhelm allowed the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to lapse, leaving Russia diplomatically exposed.
• 1891 onwards: French banks financed Russian railway and industrial projects, building economic ties.
• August 1892: secret Franco-Russian military convention drafted.
• January 1894: the Franco-Russian Alliance was formally ratified, ending French isolation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the diary of Prince Bernhard von Bülow, German diplomat and later chancellor, recorded in 1893 and published in his memoirs.
‘We have allowed the wire to Russia to be cut. The Tsar will not forget. France, with her wealth and her hatred of us, will buy what Berlin would not give. The result must be an entente of opposites — republic and autocracy — against us.’

Source C: An extract from a leading article in The Times of London, 5 January 1894, on the announcement of closer Franco-Russian ties.
‘British policy must reckon with a new fact. The European balance has shifted. While London has held to splendid isolation, Paris and St Petersburg have built a partnership of mutual defence. The continent is no longer arranged as Bismarck left it.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Franco-Russian Alliance on European diplomacy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Bülow blames Wilhelm for letting the Reinsurance Treaty lapse and predicts a Franco-Russian alignment despite ideological differences. Provenance: a contemporary diary by a senior German diplomat, but published later as memoirs which can be self-serving. Own knowledge: the Reinsurance Treaty did lapse in 1890; French loans to Russia began in 1891; the alliance was ratified in January 1894 — confirming Bülow’s prediction.
Source C — Content: argues British isolation looks weaker because the European balance has shifted. Provenance: leading article in a major British newspaper at the moment of the alliance’s announcement — informed contemporary commentary, but reflecting a particular British liberal viewpoint. Own knowledge: by the late 1890s Britain was reconsidering Splendid Isolation, leading eventually to the 1904 Entente Cordiale.
Judgement: B is highly useful as insider commentary on German strategic error but limited by its memoir provenance; C is useful as informed contemporary reaction but speaks only to British perceptions.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a private letter by Tsar Alexander III to his foreign minister, dated December 1893, drawn from the Russian state archives in St Petersburg.
‘We must not be alone. The Germans have grown arrogant under their new emperor and the chancellor in Vienna will follow Berlin into any quarrel. France, though a republic, is loyal to her word and rich enough to support the army we need. We will sign.’

Source E: An extract from a 1895 cartoon caption in the German satirical magazine Simplicissimus, depicting Marianne (France) and a Russian bear shaking hands across a chasm.
‘Strange bedfellows: a republic that beheaded its king, a tsar who fears nothing more than republics. Yet they have found one common cause — us.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The decisions of Wilhelm II were the main reason European diplomacy shifted between 1890 and 1894.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D suggests Russia signed the alliance partly because German behaviour under Wilhelm had become unreliable.
• Source E captures how unlikely the Franco-Russian partnership would have been without German blunders.
• Wilhelm dismissed Bismarck (1890), let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse (1890) and pursued an aggressive style — directly creating the diplomatic gap France filled.
Challenging the claim:
• France’s long-standing desire to recover Alsace-Lorraine was a structural cause independent of Wilhelm.
• Russian industrial backwardness made French capital attractive regardless of Berlin’s mistakes.
• Bismarck’s system was already strained — his Three Emperors’ League had collapsed in 1887 over Balkan rivalries.
Judgement: Wilhelm’s decisions accelerated the shift, but underlying French and Russian interests would likely have produced a partnership eventually.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British Foreign Office briefing paper to Lord Salisbury, dated February 1894, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘Information from St Petersburg confirms that the military convention between France and Russia is now ratified by the Tsar and the President of the Republic. The instrument is defensive in form but its effect is plain: the Continent is divided into two armed groups. Britain may continue to stand apart, but the cost of doing so will rise year by year.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying British reactions to the Franco-Russian Alliance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: The source shows that British policymakers already saw the alliance as dividing Europe into ‘two armed groups’ — useful evidence that London understood the strategic shift even while continuing Splendid Isolation.
• Provenance: It is a confidential briefing paper from the Foreign Office to the prime minister — likely to express genuine professional analysis without diplomatic varnish.
• Own knowledge: This matches the trajectory of British policy — within ten years Britain would sign the Entente Cordiale (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Convention (1907), abandoning isolation altogether.
• Limitation: The paper reflects one official’s analysis at a single moment; it does not show the full range of cabinet opinion.

lessons.title: The Alliance System and Splendid Isolation
lessons.description: Triple Alliance, Entente Cordiale and Triple Entente — how Europe split into two camps by 1907.
lessons.content_html:
Two Blocs Take Shape

By 1907 Europe was divided into two armed groupings. On one side stood the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. On the other stood the Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia. Neither alliance was identical to the other. The Triple Alliance was a formal defensive treaty with clear obligations; the Triple Entente was a looser network of agreements settling colonial disputes and aligning policy. But the diplomatic effect was the same: a crisis between any two states risked dragging in their partners, and statesmen on both sides had to plan for a coalition war.

Key Fact

By 1907 Europe was split into two camps: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy — finalised 1882) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia — completed 1907). The first was a formal defensive treaty; the second was a network of bilateral agreements.

The Triple Alliance, 1882

The Triple Alliance grew out of Bismarck’s diplomacy. Germany and Austria-Hungary had signed the Dual Alliance in 1879, pledging mutual defence against Russia. In 1882 Italy joined them. Italy was a relative newcomer to European diplomacy, unified only in 1871, and resented French ambitions in North Africa — especially the French occupation of Tunisia in 1881, which Italy had hoped to claim. The treaty bound each state to come to the others’ aid if attacked by two or more Great Powers, and obliged them to remain neutral in other conflicts. It was renewed every few years; in 1902, however, Italy quietly signed a separate agreement promising France neutrality if attacked by Germany — a hint that Italian commitment was not as deep as the treaty implied.

Italy’s commitment to the Triple Alliance was always shallow. Many Italians regarded Austria-Hungary as the ‘hereditary enemy’ because it controlled Italian-speaking territories such as Trento and Trieste — the unredeemed lands or Italia irredenta. When war came in 1914, Italy declared its neutrality on the technical ground that the war was offensive, not defensive. In 1915 Italy switched sides, joining the Entente in the secret Treaty of London in return for promised territorial gains. The Triple Alliance was always a marriage of convenience.

Britain Abandons Splendid Isolation

By 1900 Britain’s policy of Splendid Isolation looked increasingly risky. The Boer War (1899-1902) had shown how unpopular Britain was on the continent — cartoons in French and German papers mocked British soldiers and sympathy ran with the Boers. The Royal Navy was being challenged by a German naval programme. Britain’s commitments stretched from Canada to India to Africa, and isolation no longer guaranteed security. The first step away was the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902, easing Britain’s position in the Far East. Then came the bigger shift: a settlement with France.

The Entente Cordiale of 1904

In April 1904 Britain and France signed the Entente Cordiale. It was not a military alliance. The agreement settled colonial quarrels: Britain recognised French interests in Morocco, France recognised British control of Egypt, and the two powers tidied up disputes in West Africa, Madagascar and Newfoundland. King Edward VII’s state visit to Paris in 1903 had warmed the public mood. The signed agreement looked technical, but its political meaning was huge. Two states that had been on the brink of war over the Sudan as recently as 1898 (the Fashoda Incident) were now settling differences and aligning their diplomacy. Germany found this profoundly worrying.

The Anglo-Russian Convention and the Triple Entente of 1907

Britain and Russia were also rivals — the ‘Great Game’ over Persia, Afghanistan and the approaches to India had run for decades. After Russia’s humiliation in the Russo-Japanese War (1905) it was looking for European support, while Britain was looking to settle its imperial frontiers. The Anglo-Russian Convention of August 1907 carved up Persia into spheres of influence, recognised Afghanistan as a British zone and settled disputes over Tibet. Combined with the existing Franco-Russian Alliance and the Entente Cordiale, this completed the triangle. Historians from 1907 onwards spoke of the Triple Entente, even though the three states had no single treaty — just three bilateral agreements that pointed the same way.

Alliances are usually intended to deter war — if a state knows attacking one country means fighting two, it should think twice. But the European system of 1907 had a darker logic. Once both blocs were locked in, a small incident between any two states could trigger a chain reaction. Military planners on both sides built mobilisation timetables that assumed coalition war from day one. By 1914 these plans — especially Germany’s Schlieffen Plan and Russia’s mobilisation against Austria and Germany simultaneously — would mean that diplomacy had only days to defuse a crisis before military timetables took over. Christopher Clark’s study The Sleepwalkers argues that this is not the same as alliances ‘causing’ the war, but the rigidity they imposed left far less room for compromise.

Key Fact

The Triple Entente was built from three bilateral agreements: the Franco-Russian Alliance (1894), the Entente Cordiale (1904, settling colonial disputes between Britain and France), and the Anglo-Russian Convention (1907, settling disputes over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet). It was a network, not a single treaty.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Narrative Account on the alliance system, examiners want a chain of cause and consequence, not a list of treaties. Use connectives such as ‘this prompted’, ‘as a result’, ‘in response to which’ to link three or four events together. A strong answer might trace: Bismarck’s isolation of France → Wilhelm’s decision to drop Russia → the Franco-Russian Alliance → British Splendid Isolation under pressure → the Entente Cordiale → the Anglo-Russian Convention completing the Triple Entente. Three to four linked steps with precise dates earns top marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Triple Alliance of 1882 (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) was a formal defensive treaty with clear obligations — though Italy’s commitment was always shallow.
  • Britain abandoned Splendid Isolation in stages: the Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902), the Entente Cordiale with France (1904), and the Anglo-Russian Convention (1907).
  • By 1907 Europe was divided into two camps. The alliances did not cause war directly, but they created the rigid coalition logic that limited diplomacy when crisis struck.

Study Source A.

‘The agreement signed in April with His Britannic Majesty’s government is not an alliance — it engages neither army nor navy. It is, however, the end of a century of mistrust. From this day forward the rivalries that consumed our two peoples in Egypt, Morocco and Newfoundland are at an end.’

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Sir Eyre Crowe, senior Foreign Office adviser, on the state of relations with Germany, dated 1 January 1907, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘The German menace is not the policy of any single statesman but the structural ambition of a state that has outgrown its earlier role. Britain has slowly responded — through Tokyo, Paris, and now St Petersburg. The result is not yet an alliance, but the lines of cooperation are unmistakable.’

Source C: An extract from a 1908 article in the Vienna newspaper Neue Freie Presse, on Anglo-Russian relations.
‘London and St Petersburg, divided for half a century by the Great Game, have signed an agreement carving up Persia between them. Berlin must understand the meaning of what has happened: the encirclement is complete.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying European reactions to the formation of the Triple Entente. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Crowe argues the German threat is structural, and Britain has responded through agreements with Japan, France and Russia. Provenance: a confidential Foreign Office memorandum by a senior official, intended for cabinet readers — likely to express genuine analysis. Own knowledge: the so-called ‘Crowe Memorandum’ was an influential statement of British anti-German thinking in 1907.
Source C — Content: argues the Anglo-Russian Convention completes Germany’s ‘encirclement’. Provenance: a leading Austro-Hungarian newspaper — sympathetic to the German viewpoint, useful for showing how the Triple Alliance side perceived the Entente. Own knowledge: German leaders did speak of Einkreisung (encirclement) from this period; the perception, accurate or not, shaped German strategy.
Judgement: B is highly useful as insider British analysis but reflects one current of Foreign Office opinion; C is useful as Central European reaction but rhetorical and one-sided.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from the diary of Sir Edward Grey, British Foreign Secretary, dated August 1907, drawn from the Grey Papers held at the British Library.
‘With the convention now signed at St Petersburg, the persistent quarrels in Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet are at an end. Britain has cleared its imperial frontiers. The wider effect is plain: a London-Paris-Petersburg axis, however informal, now stands across the path of any state that imagines a continental free hand.’

Source E: An extract from a 1907 cartoon caption in the German satirical magazine Kladderadatsch, depicting John Bull, Marianne and a Russian bear shaking hands in a circle around a watching Kaiser.
‘Three doors close at once. The young man at the centre is left to wonder whether his friends will open theirs.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The completion of the Triple Entente in 1907 was the main reason Europe drifted towards war.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows London openly recognised the Triple Entente as a check on continental ambitions.
• Source E captures the German fear of encirclement that pushed Berlin towards more aggressive policies.
• The Entente made it harder to localise crises — any clash between two great powers risked dragging in their partners.

• Underlying causes — Anglo-German naval rivalry, Slav nationalism, Austro-Russian Balkan conflict — were independent of the Entente.

lessons.title: Anglo-German Rivalry: Weltpolitik and the Naval Race
lessons.description: Wilhelm II’s Weltpolitik, the Tirpitz naval programme, and the dreadnought race that poisoned.
lessons.content_html:
Weltpolitik: A New German World Policy

When Bismarck was forced out in 1890, Germany’s new chancellors and the Kaiser made a decisive break with his cautious, continental focus. The new doctrine was Weltpolitik — world policy. Wilhelm II declared that Germany must take its ‘place in the sun’: a global empire to match Britain’s, a battle fleet to project power across oceans, and a louder voice in every international quarrel. The phrase came from a 1897 Reichstag speech by foreign minister Bernhard von Bülow: ‘We do not want to put anyone in the shade, but we too demand a place in the sun.’ Where Bismarck had been content with a satisfied Germany at the heart of Europe, Wilhelm wanted Germany to be a global power on the model of Britain.

Key Fact

Weltpolitik was the post-Bismarck German policy of seeking world power status — through colonies, a battle fleet and a global voice. Articulated by Bülow in his 1897 ‘place in the sun’ speech, it broke decisively with Bismarck’s European caution.

Colonial Friction

Germany was a latecomer to imperialism. By 1900 the world’s best colonial real estate was already taken by Britain, France, Russia and the smaller European powers. The German empire that did exist — in Cameroon, German East Africa (now Tanzania), South-West Africa (now Namibia), Togo and Pacific islands — was modest and often unprofitable. Germans demanding more colonies clashed repeatedly with the established empires. The Kruger Telegram of January 1896, in which Wilhelm congratulated the South African Boer leader Paul Kruger on repelling a British raid, infuriated London. The Boxer Rebellion of 1900 brought German troops into China, but again exposed how far Germany trailed Britain and France in global reach. Each colonial irritation deepened British distrust.

Wilhelm II was not a stable diplomatic actor. He gave provocative speeches without warning his ministers, sent intemperate telegrams to foreign leaders, and once gave an interview to Britain’s Daily Telegraph in 1908 that simultaneously offended Britain, France and Russia. Historians disagree about how much weight to put on personality. Christopher Clark’s The Sleepwalkers argues structural rivalry mattered more than the Kaiser’s outbursts; older accounts emphasise his erratic temperament. The truth is probably both: Wilhelm’s instincts pointed Germany down a confrontational path that the country’s industrial weight then made dangerous.

Tirpitz and the Naval Laws

The most consequential strand of Weltpolitik was naval. Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz, appointed Naval Secretary in 1897, believed Germany needed a battle fleet large enough to threaten Britain’s. His ‘risk theory’ argued that even a fleet smaller than the Royal Navy could deter British action: Britain would not dare risk losing so many capital ships even in victory. The First German Naval Law of 1898 set out a programme of nineteen battleships. The Second Naval Law of 1900 doubled the planned fleet. By 1914 Germany would build sixteen of the biggest new warships — the dreadnoughts — against Britain’s twenty-nine.

HMS Dreadnought, 1906

In February 1906 Britain launched HMS Dreadnought. The ship was a revolution: ten 12-inch guns where older battleships had four, steam turbine engines for unprecedented speed, and heavier armour than anything afloat. The launch made every other battleship in the world — including the Royal Navy’s — obsolete in a single afternoon. Britain hoped to use its industrial lead to outbuild Germany; Germany saw an opening to start the race more or less even. Both sides accelerated. The Anglo-German naval race had begun.

Public opinion in both countries inflamed the rivalry. In Britain, the navalist slogan ‘We want eight, and we won’t wait!’ (a demand for eight new dreadnoughts in 1909) became a genuine political force. In Germany, the Navy League agitated for ever-larger budgets and presented the fleet as proof of German modernity. By 1912 the cost of the race forced Britain to negotiate. The Haldane Mission, a British attempt to slow construction in exchange for political concessions, came back empty-handed.

Historians disagree on this. Some, including Paul Kennedy in The Rise of Anglo-German Antagonism, argue the naval race was the central irritant that pushed Britain into the Entente camp. Others, including Christopher Clark, treat it as one factor among many. What is clear is that the race did not directly cause the war — in 1914 Britain went to war over Belgium, not battleships. But the race had soured Anglo-German relations to the point where, when crisis struck, Britain had no inclination to give Germany the benefit of the doubt. Naval rivalry built the political climate, even if it did not pull the trigger.

Personality versus Structure

A useful exam question is whether Wilhelm II personally caused this rivalry, or whether structural forces — the rise of German industry, the desire for empire among the German middle class, the strategic logic of a powerful state on the European continent — would have produced something similar under any leader. Both sides have evidence. The Kruger Telegram and the Daily Telegraph interview are clearly individual blunders. But the Tirpitz programme had broad political support and would have continued under most plausible chancellors. Strong essays acknowledge both: Wilhelm gave the policy its tone and damage, but the structural rivalry was real and would have caused friction even with a different emperor on the throne.

Key Fact

HMS Dreadnought launched in February 1906. With its all-big-gun layout and turbine engines, it made every existing battleship obsolete — resetting the naval race and giving Germany a chance to compete from a more even starting line.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark Source Utility question on Anglo-German rivalry, examiners want all three of content, provenance and your own knowledge applied to each source. A common trap is to dismiss a source as ‘biased’ without using its content or your knowledge. A propaganda poster is still useful evidence of the message authorities wanted citizens to absorb. Always ask: useful for what? A source can be highly useful for studying public opinion even if unreliable as a record of facts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Weltpolitik replaced Bismarck’s continental caution with global ambition — colonies, a battle fleet and a louder German voice in international affairs.
  • The Tirpitz Naval Laws (1898, 1900 and later) and the launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906 ignited an Anglo-German naval race that ran without compromise until the war.
  • Wilhelm II’s personality made the policy more provocative, but the structural rivalry between a rising industrial Germany and a global Britain was the deeper cause.

Source E: An extract from a 1909 cartoon caption in the British satirical magazine Punch, showing John Bull and Wilhelm II hammering rival warships in adjacent shipyards.
‘The friendly competition. Each man swears he wants peace; each man hammers harder. The bill, however, will be paid by their citizens.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The personality of Wilhelm II was the main reason for the breakdown of Anglo-German relations before 1914.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.

Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source E captures the rivalry as competition between two leaders — placing personality at the centre.
• Wilhelm’s erratic interventions (Kruger Telegram 1896, Daily Telegraph interview 1908) repeatedly damaged Anglo-German relations.
• His sponsorship of Tirpitz and the Naval Laws gave the rivalry a personal stamp.

• Source D shows even the Royal Navy treated this as structural — a clash of strategic interests, not personalities.
• The Naval Laws had broad political support across German parties; the Navy League agitated regardless of Wilhelm.
• German industrial growth and the desire for colonies pre-dated Wilhelm’s reign.
Judgement: Wilhelm’s personality made the rivalry more provocative, but the underlying clash between a rising industrial Germany and a global Britain was structural and would have produced friction under any plausible leader.

• Limitation: It reflects one official’s view at a particular date; it does not capture the role personalities played in turning structural rivalry into open hostility.

lessons.title: Crisis Points: Morocco 1905 and 1911, Bosnia 1908-09
lessons.description: The Tangier and Agadir crises and the Bosnian Annexation — three pre-war shocks that hardened the.
lessons.content_html:
Three Crises, Three Rehearsals for War

Between 1905 and 1911 Europe lived through three diplomatic shocks that did not start a war but came uncomfortably close. Each one hardened the alliance blocs and rehearsed the brinkmanship that would explode in 1914. The First Moroccan Crisis of 1905-06, the Bosnian Annexation Crisis of 1908-09 and the Second Moroccan (Agadir) Crisis of 1911 each began as a local dispute and ended as a continental confrontation. By the third crisis, all sides were pulling stronger on their alliance partners and rehearsing military mobilisation timetables. The system was learning, dangerously, how to escalate.

Key Fact

Three pre-war crises shook the alliance system: the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) tightened the Entente Cordiale, the Bosnian Annexation Crisis (1908-09) humiliated Russia and angered Serbia, and the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911) brought Britain firmly behind France.

The First Moroccan Crisis: Tangier, 1905

In March 1905 Wilhelm II landed at Tangier on the Moroccan coast and gave a speech declaring support for Moroccan independence and for ‘equal commercial opportunities’. The intervention was deliberately provocative. Under the Entente Cordiale of 1904 Britain had recognised French interests in Morocco; Wilhelm wanted to test whether the Entente was a real diplomatic bloc or just words on paper. France was thrown into panic. The crisis was referred to an international conference at Algeciras in early 1906. There Germany found itself with only Austria-Hungary’s support; Britain, Russia, Italy, Spain and the United States all backed France. The result was a diplomatic defeat for Germany — the opposite of what Wilhelm had intended.

Germany’s mistake was to call for a conference assuming international opinion would back ‘open door’ trade against French preferences. Instead, Britain and Russia closed ranks behind France, Italy quietly drifted further from the Triple Alliance, and even the United States declined to support the German line. The conference recognised French and Spanish predominance in Morocco. Worse, it accelerated Anglo-French military cooperation: secret staff talks between the British and French armies began in early 1906 specifically because of the Tangier crisis. Germany emerged from a crisis it had started in a worse position than when it began.

The Bosnian Annexation Crisis, 1908-09

Bosnia had been administered by Austria-Hungary since the 1878 Congress of Berlin, but technically remained part of the Ottoman Empire. In October 1908, exploiting Ottoman weakness during the Young Turk Revolution, Austria-Hungary formally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina. The move outraged Serbia, which had hoped to incorporate Bosnia’s large Slav population into a future Greater Serbia. Russia, the traditional protector of Slav peoples, had been led to believe by Austrian foreign minister Aehrenthal that compensation would be offered — but in the event Russia got nothing. Russia’s humiliation deepened when Germany backed Austria-Hungary unconditionally and effectively forced Russia to accept the annexation in March 1909. The Tsar’s government swore that Russia would not be humiliated again.

The Second Moroccan Crisis: Agadir, 1911

In April 1911 French troops occupied the Moroccan city of Fez to suppress an uprising. Germany seized the opportunity to demand compensation. In July 1911 the German gunboat Panther appeared off the southern Moroccan port of Agadir, ostensibly to protect German citizens. There were no German citizens in Agadir. The gesture — later called the Agadir Crisis — was a transparent piece of gunboat diplomacy. France refused to be intimidated. More importantly, Britain came down emphatically on the French side. In a famous Mansion House speech that July, Chancellor of the Exchequer David Lloyd George warned that Britain would not accept being ‘treated as if of no account’. The crisis ended with a humiliating climbdown for Germany: a small piece of the French Congo as compensation for nothing.

After Algeciras, Anglo-French military staff talks began. After Bosnia, Russia accelerated army modernisation and pledged not to back down again over Slav interests. After Agadir, the British Cabinet authorised secret naval cooperation with France — agreeing that the French navy would concentrate in the Mediterranean while the Royal Navy guaranteed the Channel. Each crisis ratcheted the alliance commitments up a notch. By 1912 the blocs were tighter than they had been before; the room for the Great Powers to step back from a Balkan crisis was visibly narrower. Christopher Clark calls this period the ‘polarisation’ of European politics.

The Balkan Wars, 1912-13

Tension in the Balkans then turned into open war. In October 1912 the Balkan League — Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro — attacked the Ottoman Empire and won quickly. The First Balkan War nearly doubled Serbia’s territory. The Second Balkan War of June-August 1913 saw the victors fight over the spoils, with Bulgaria attacking its former allies and being defeated in turn. Although the wars stayed local, they alarmed Austria-Hungary by leaving Serbia much stronger; intensified Russian backing for Slav states; and warned Germany that the next Balkan flashpoint might be harder to contain. The Balkan Wars are not crises in the same sense as Tangier, Bosnia or Agadir, but they sharpen the picture of how dangerous south-eastern Europe had become by 1914.

Key Fact

Each crisis tightened the alliance system. Algeciras produced Anglo-French staff talks; Bosnia humiliated Russia and pushed Serbia towards the Black Hand; Agadir brought Britain into the open on France’s side and produced an Anglo-French naval agreement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on the pre-war crises, do not simply describe each one. Show how they fit together. Each crisis should connect to the next: the lesson Germany drew from Algeciras shaped the Agadir gamble; the humiliation Russia felt over Bosnia shaped its decisions in 1914. Use connectives like ‘the lesson Berlin drew from this’ or ‘in response to which Russia’. The marker is looking for an analytical chain, not three separate paragraphs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) ended at Algeciras as a German diplomatic defeat — and triggered Anglo-French military staff talks.
  • The Bosnian Annexation Crisis (1908-09) humiliated Russia, hardened Serbian nationalism and demonstrated that Germany would back Austria-Hungary unconditionally.
  • The Second Moroccan Crisis at Agadir (1911) brought Britain firmly behind France and produced a secret Anglo-French naval agreement — tightening the alliance blocs further.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1906 British Foreign Office despatch from Sir Charles Hardinge to the Foreign Secretary, written during the Algeciras Conference, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘Germany came to this conference expecting allies; she has found only Vienna at her side. The other powers — including the United States — have closed ranks behind France. Berlin will leave the conference with less than she had before, and with a clear lesson taught about the strength of the Entente.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Hardinge gives for Germany’s position at Algeciras.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Germany was diplomatically isolated — only Austria-Hungary supported her (‘only Vienna at her side’).
• The other powers closed ranks behind France, including the United States.
• Germany would leave with less than she came for — a clear diplomatic defeat.
• The crisis demonstrated the strength of the Entente.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Bosnian Annexation Crisis from October 1908 to March 1909.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Young Turk Revolution, Aehrenthal’s diplomacy, Russian outrage, German ultimatum, Russian climbdown); reaches the March 1909 outcome through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• Summer 1908: The Young Turk Revolution weakened Ottoman authority, opening an opportunity in the Balkans.
• October 1908: Austria-Hungary unilaterally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina.
• Late 1908: Russia and Serbia protested furiously; Russia had been told by Aehrenthal compensation would be offered.
• Winter 1908-09: Russia mobilised diplomatically but was militarily unready after the 1905 Russo-Japanese defeat.
• March 1909: Germany issued an effective ultimatum demanding Russia accept the annexation.
• March 1909: Russia backed down — humiliated but vowing not to retreat again over Slav interests.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a speech by David Lloyd George at the Mansion House, City of London, 21 July 1911, drawn from contemporary press reports of the Agadir Crisis.
‘If a situation were to be forced upon us in which peace could only be preserved by the surrender of the great and beneficent position Britain has won, then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation intolerable for a great country like ours to endure.’

Source C: An extract from a 1911 Berlin newspaper editorial in the Berliner Tageblatt, on Lloyd George’s Mansion House speech.
‘The British minister speaks as if our gunboat at Agadir threatened London itself. We sought a colonial compensation, not a war. Yet British ministers have chosen to wave the flag and rattle the sword. The lesson Germany must draw is plain: the Entente is closer than its founders pretended.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Agadir Crisis on European diplomacy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Lloyd George signals Britain will not be ‘treated as of no account’ — a clear public warning to Germany. Provenance: a major Cabinet minister giving a high-profile speech in the City — designed for European ears. Own knowledge: the speech was widely understood across Europe as Britain backing France in the crisis; it shocked Berlin.
Source C — Content: argues Britain has overreacted to a colonial gesture, but acknowledges the Entente is stronger than it appears. Provenance: a leading liberal Berlin newspaper — useful for German public reaction, though shaped by domestic outrage. Own knowledge: the German climbdown that summer and the Anglo-French naval agreement that followed bear out the source’s implicit conclusion.
Judgement: B is highly useful as the public British warning; C is useful as German public reaction. Used together they capture the moment alliance lines hardened in public view.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a private letter by Russian foreign minister Alexander Izvolsky to the Russian ambassador in Vienna, dated April 1909, drawn from the Russian state archives.
‘We have been deceived. Aehrenthal promised consultation; we received an annexation. Berlin then chose to threaten us with mobilisation. Russia will not — cannot — fight today. But this humiliation will not be forgotten. The next time the Slavs of the Balkans look to us, we shall not turn away.’

Source E: An extract from a 1909 cartoon caption in the French satirical magazine L’Assiette au Beurre, showing a Russian bear handcuffed to a Serbian peasant under a watching Austrian eagle.
‘Two friends of the Slav cause — neither free to act. The eagle waits to see who moves first.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The Bosnian Annexation Crisis was the most damaging of the three pre-war crises for European peace.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows Russian foreign policy permanently scarred by the humiliation — the pledge ‘we shall not turn away’ shaped 1914.
• Source E captures the Slav frustration that fed Serbian secret-society activity and the Black Hand.
• Bosnia hardened Russian and Serbian commitment in a way Algeciras and Agadir did not — both later Moroccan crises were colonial, not existential.
Challenging the claim:
• Algeciras began the Anglo-French military staff talks that turned the Entente into a quasi-military partnership.
• Agadir produced the Anglo-French naval agreement that made British military commitment to France semi-automatic.
• The Balkan Wars of 1912-13 then made the south-east European tinder more dangerous still.
Judgement: Bosnia was uniquely damaging for Russo-Austrian and Russo-German trust, but the Moroccan crises shaped the western coalition. Each contributed to a different vulnerability.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British First Sea Lord Sir Arthur Wilson, dated August 1911, drawn from the Wilson Papers held at the Royal Naval Museum, Portsmouth.
‘The Cabinet has authorised cooperation with the French navy in the Mediterranean. Should war come, the French fleet will hold the Mediterranean and we shall hold the Channel and the North Sea. The arrangement is informal but unmistakable. After Agadir, no minister can pretend the Entente is a thing of words alone.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the impact of the Agadir Crisis on Anglo-French cooperation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: The source records a concrete naval arrangement — French fleet in the Mediterranean, Royal Navy in the Channel — useful evidence that the Entente had become semi-military.
• Provenance: A diary entry by the First Sea Lord — the senior professional head of the Royal Navy, with direct access to Cabinet decisions.
• Own knowledge: The 1912 Anglo-French Naval Convention formalised exactly this arrangement, demonstrating how Agadir had pushed Britain over a threshold.
• Limitation: One Admiral’s diary, however senior, does not capture wider Cabinet debate — Lord Morley and others were uneasy with the commitment.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the three pre-war crises reshaped European alliances between 1905 and 1911.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 1911 outcome through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• March 1905: Wilhelm II’s Tangier landing opened the First Moroccan Crisis.
• 1906: Algeciras Conference produced a German diplomatic defeat and Anglo-French military staff talks.
• October 1908: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia, infuriating Russia and Serbia.
• March 1909: German ultimatum forced Russian climbdown — Russia vowed not to back down again.
• July 1911: German gunboat Panther arrived at Agadir, sparking the Second Moroccan Crisis.
• Late 1911 - 1912: Lloyd George’s Mansion House speech and the Anglo-French Naval Convention completed the British shift towards France.

lessons.title: Sarajevo and the July Crisis
lessons.description: Princip’s shots, the blank cheque and the cascade of mobilisations between 28 June and 4 August 1914.
lessons.content_html:
Sarajevo, 28 June 1914

Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, arrived in Sarajevo on the morning of 28 June 1914 to inspect Bosnian military manoeuvres. The date was provocative: it was the anniversary of the medieval Battle of Kosovo, a sacred day in Serbian nationalism. Six young assassins from the secret Serbian society the Black Hand had crossed the border to kill him. The first attempt — a bomb — failed. The Archduke decided to visit hospital to see the wounded. His driver took a wrong turn and stopped to reverse directly in front of one of the conspirators, Gavrilo Princip, who fired two shots. Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were both dead within minutes.

Key Fact

On 28 June 1914 Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip, acting for the Black Hand secret society, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. The assassination triggered the July Crisis — but it was the trigger, not the cause, of the war.

Slav Nationalism and the Long Background

Slav nationalism had been a structural problem for Austria-Hungary for decades. The empire ruled millions of Czechs, Poles, Croats, Slovenes, Slovaks and Bosnian Serbs alongside its German and Hungarian core. Many of these peoples wanted national independence or union with neighbouring Slav states. Serbia, freshly enlarged by the 1912-13 Balkan Wars, made itself the patron of Slav independence. The Bosnian Annexation of 1908 had infuriated Serbian opinion; the Black Hand, founded in 1911, organised cross-border activity to undermine Habsburg rule. For Vienna, Serbia was an existential threat, not just a small neighbour.

A common student error is to write that the assassination ‘caused’ the First World War. It did not. The deeper causes — the alliance system, Anglo-German naval rivalry, Slav nationalism in Austria-Hungary, the militarisation of European planning — had been building for two decades. The shots in Sarajevo were the spark that ignited an already prepared bonfire. Other shots in 1914 might equally have produced a war — or might not have, if the alliance system had been less rigid. Christopher Clark’s The Sleepwalkers argues European leaders did not consciously choose war but allowed themselves to be carried by their own commitments and miscalculations to the brink and then over it.

The Blank Cheque, 5 July 1914

The Austro-Hungarian government in Vienna decided within days that Serbia must be punished. But it needed German support. On 5 July 1914 the Austrian ambassador presented Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bethmann-Hollweg with a request for backing in any action against Serbia. Wilhelm gave it: the so-called blank cheque. Germany pledged unconditional support. The cheque mattered because Vienna had hesitated before; with Berlin behind it, Austria-Hungary felt free to risk a wider war. Some historians, following Fritz Fischer’s controversial 1961 thesis Griff nach der Weltmacht, argue the blank cheque shows Germany deliberately welcomed war. Others, including Clark, argue Berlin expected localisation and gravely misjudged.

The Ultimatum, 23 July

On 23 July 1914 Austria-Hungary delivered to Serbia an ultimatum so severe it was designed to be rejected. It demanded Serbian suppression of anti-Austrian publications, dissolution of nationalist societies, dismissal of named officials, and the right of Austrian officials to enter Serbia to investigate the assassination. Serbia was given 48 hours. Serbia, advised by Russia, accepted almost every demand — but rejected the right of Austrian officials to operate on Serbian soil as a violation of sovereignty. Austria-Hungary declared the reply unsatisfactory and broke off diplomatic relations on 25 July. War was declared on Serbia on 28 July, exactly one month after Sarajevo.

Mobilisation Cascade, 30 July - 4 August

From 30 July events accelerated faster than diplomats could keep up. Russia ordered partial mobilisation in support of Serbia, then full mobilisation on 30 July when partial proved technically impossible. Germany, whose Schlieffen Plan required defeating France before Russia could fully mobilise, demanded Russia stand down. When Russia refused, Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August, on France on 3 August, and invaded neutral Belgium on the way to Paris on 4 August. Britain, citing the 1839 Treaty of London guaranteeing Belgian neutrality, declared war on Germany the same evening. Within seven days a Balkan dispute had become a continental war.

Several factors made July 1914 different from earlier crises. Mobilisation timetables had grown so detailed that any delay risked strategic disaster — military leaders pressed politicians to mobilise quickly. Germany and Russia had no direct telephone link; messages travelled through diplomatic channels measured in hours. Each side believed the other intended war and acted on the worst-case assumption. Sir Edward Grey’s British proposal for a four-power conference was rejected by Germany on 27 July. By the time Wilhelm and Tsar Nicholas II exchanged personal ‘Willy-Nicky’ telegrams begging each other to reconsider, the German army was already on the move. The crisis showed how rapidly the alliance system could turn a regional dispute into general war.

Key Fact

The July Crisis ran from 28 June to 4 August 1914. Key dates: blank cheque (5 July), ultimatum to Serbia (23 July), Austrian declaration of war on Serbia (28 July), Russian full mobilisation (30 July), German declarations on Russia (1 August) and France (3 August), and British declaration on Germany (4 August) after the invasion of Belgium.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark Source-Based Essay on the July Crisis, examiners want a sustained argument that engages with the specific claim and uses both sources as a springboard, not as the centre of the answer. Treat the source as one piece of evidence and bring in your own contextual detail (Black Hand, blank cheque, ultimatum terms, Schlieffen logic, Belgian neutrality). A common trap is to spend too long describing the sources and run out of time for analysis — aim to spend roughly half your time on argument and contextual evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Sarajevo assassination was the trigger of the war, not its cause — deeper alliance, naval, nationalist and military-planning tensions had been building for decades.
  • Germany’s blank cheque on 5 July emboldened Austria-Hungary to issue an ultimatum designed to be rejected.
  • The cascade of mobilisations between 30 July and 4 August turned a Balkan dispute into a general European war within a week, propelled by alliance commitments and rigid military timetables.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a telegram by German chancellor Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg to the German ambassador in Vienna, dated 6 July 1914, drawn from the Auswärtiges Amt diplomatic archives in Berlin.
‘His Majesty has assured Vienna of Germany’s steadfast support in any action she may consider necessary against Serbia. The chancellor concurs. Whatever Vienna decides, Berlin will stand behind her.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons the source shows the importance of the German blank cheque.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Germany pledged ‘steadfast support’ to Austria-Hungary against Serbia.
• The pledge was unconditional — ‘whatever Vienna decides, Berlin will stand behind her’.
• Both Wilhelm II (‘His Majesty’) and Bethmann-Hollweg endorsed it, making it official German policy.
• It encouraged Vienna to act decisively rather than negotiate.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Europe moved from the assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 to a general European war by 4 August.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (assassination, blank cheque, ultimatum, Serbian reply, Russian mobilisation, German declarations, Belgian invasion); reaches the British declaration through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 28 June 1914: Princip shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo.
• 5 July 1914: Germany gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the personal diary of Russian foreign minister Sergei Sazonov, dated 30 July 1914, drawn from the Sazonov Papers held at the Russian state archives.
‘The Tsar has signed the order for general mobilisation. He hesitated through the morning, weighed by what he called the responsibility of millions of lives. Yet partial mobilisation, our generals confirm, is technically impossible. Berlin will use this against us. We have no choice — to retreat now would be to repeat 1909.’

Source C: An extract from a 1925 memoir by British Foreign Secretary Sir Edward Grey, recalling the events of late July 1914 and published as Twenty-Five Years.
‘In all the years since, I have come back to those last days of July and asked whether anything could have stopped what came. The fault lay not with one man, but with the system: alliances that bound, timetables that tightened, ministers that telegraphed past one another. We were all of us prisoners of arrangements made years before.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why diplomacy failed in July 1914. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Sazonov captures Russian decision-making — Tsar’s hesitation, technical impossibility of partial mobilisation, fear of repeating the 1909 humiliation. Provenance: a contemporaneous private diary by the foreign minister at the heart of the crisis — likely to record genuine thinking. Own knowledge: Russia did mobilise on 30 July; the 1909 reference points to the Bosnian humiliation that Russia had vowed never to repeat.
Source C — Content: Grey argues the system, not individuals, made war inevitable. Provenance: a memoir written eleven years later — useful for considered reflection but shaped by hindsight and self-justification (Grey faced criticism for failing to deter Germany).
Judgement: B is highly useful for the immediate Russian decision; C is useful for considered later analysis but should not be taken as objective. Used together they capture both the granular pressures and the structural picture.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from Wilhelm II’s personal notes on the Austrian ultimatum to Serbia, dated 28 July 1914 after seeing Serbia’s reply, recorded in the official Auswärtiges Amt files.
‘A great moral victory for Austria! With this, every reason for war disappears. The reply is more than one could expect. I would never have ordered mobilisation on this basis.’

Source E: An extract from a 1914 cartoon caption in the British satirical magazine Punch, depicting two men with cigars labelled ‘Berlin’ and ‘Vienna’ leaning over a row of dominoes labelled with the names of European capitals.
‘Just to see what happens — they say. The first one falls; the rest will keep up the entertainment.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The decisions of Germany’s leaders were the main reason a Balkan crisis became a European war in 1914.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Germany’s blank cheque on 5 July emboldened Austria to issue a deliberately rejectable ultimatum.
• Source E captures the perception that Berlin and Vienna pushed the dominoes deliberately.
• The Schlieffen Plan made German mobilisation effectively unstoppable once begun.
• Fritz Fischer’s 1961 thesis argued German leaders deliberately sought war.
Challenging the claim:
• Source D suggests Wilhelm did not want war once he saw the Serbian reply — the responsibility was diffused across his ministers and military leaders.
• Russian full mobilisation on 30 July had its own logic — the Tsar wanted to avoid repeating the 1909 humiliation.
• Austrian leaders made the ultimatum decision; British failure to clarify intentions earlier may have encouraged German miscalculation.
• Christopher Clark’s Sleepwalkers thesis spreads responsibility across all the powers.
Judgement: German leaders bore disproportionate responsibility — the blank cheque and Schlieffen logic were uniquely escalatory — but the war was the product of multiple states’ choices, not Berlin’s alone.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from an exchange of telegrams between Kaiser Wilhelm II and Tsar Nicholas II, the so-called ‘Willy-Nicky’ correspondence, dated 29 July 1914 and published in the post-war diplomatic dossiers.
‘[Wilhelm to Nicholas] I beg you in the name of our old friendship to do what you can to stop your allies from going too far. [Nicholas to Wilhelm] I implore you in the name of our friendship to halt your allies before it is too late. Yours always, Nicky.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the role of personal diplomacy in the July Crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: The telegrams show the two emperors used personal ‘old friendship’ to try to halt their own ministries — useful evidence that monarchs lacked control over their own systems.
• Provenance: Direct telegrams between two heads of state at the heart of the crisis, later published as part of post-war evidence — likely to be authentic.
• Own knowledge: The Willy-Nicky exchanges did not stop the cascade. German mobilisation orders were already in motion; the Schlieffen Plan’s timetable made standing down strategically dangerous.
• Limitation: The telegrams capture only two days of the crisis and one channel of communication; they do not show the wider failure of multilateral diplomacy.

lessons.title: The Schlieffen Plan and the Battle of the Marne
lessons.description: Why Germany’s six-week plan to defeat France ran into Belgium, the BEF and Joffre’s counter-attack.
lessons.content_html:
The Strategic Problem

Germany’s strategic problem after 1894 was simple to state and almost impossible to solve. The Franco-Russian Alliance meant that any war with one would mean war with both. Germany would have to fight on two fronts — against France in the west and Russia in the east — with one army. Russia’s vast territory and slow railways meant it would take roughly six weeks to fully mobilise. France, sitting next door, could mobilise within days. From these facts, Chief of the General Staff Alfred von Schlieffen drew a single conclusion: knock France out fast, then turn east before Russia is ready.

Key Fact

The Schlieffen Plan, drafted by Alfred von Schlieffen between 1891 and 1906, aimed to defeat France within six weeks by invading through neutral Belgium and encircling Paris from the west — before turning east to face the slower-mobilising Russian army.

The Plan in Outline

Schlieffen’s 1905 design called for the bulk of the German army — roughly seven-eighths of available strength — to mass on the right wing in the north, sweep through Belgium and the Netherlands, pivot south through northern France, and encircle Paris from the west. A small left wing would hold the French along the German border in Alsace-Lorraine, even pulling back to draw the French into a trap. The whole operation was timetabled to within days. Russia would still be mobilising; France would have collapsed; Germany would then transfer troops east on its excellent railways. The plan was an act of strategic boldness: it required the violation of Belgian and Dutch neutrality, the assumption that France would attack into the trap on the German border, and the gamble that Russia would not surprise everyone by mobilising faster than expected.

Schlieffen retired in 1906 and died in 1913. His successor as Chief of the General Staff, Helmuth von Moltke (the Younger), modified the plan in important ways. He dropped the violation of Dutch neutrality (concentrating the invasion on Belgium alone), strengthened the left wing in Alsace-Lorraine and weakened the critical right wing. He also redirected some forces east in case of early Russian pressure. Schlieffen on his deathbed reportedly urged: ‘Keep the right wing strong.’ Moltke’s changes have been blamed by some historians (including Gerhard Ritter) for the plan’s failure; others argue Moltke was responding sensibly to changed circumstances. Either way, the German army that marched in August 1914 was not exactly Schlieffen’s.

August 1914: Belgium and the BEF

German troops crossed into Belgium on 4 August 1914. Belgian neutrality had been guaranteed by the 1839 Treaty of London, signed by all the Great Powers including Prussia. Britain had warned that violating Belgian neutrality would mean war; Bethmann-Hollweg dismissed the treaty as a ‘scrap of paper’. Belgium was small but its forts at Liège held out longer than expected, slowing the German advance by perhaps four critical days. Meanwhile the British Expeditionary Force — the BEF, around 100,000 well-trained regulars — crossed the Channel and met the German advance at Mons on 23 August. The BEF inflicted heavy casualties before being forced to retreat. The professional accuracy of British rifle fire so impressed the Germans that some assumed they were facing machine guns.

The Battle of the Marne, 5-12 September 1914

By early September German armies were within 50 km of Paris. The French government had fled to Bordeaux. But the German advance had over-extended itself. The right wing was weakened, troops were exhausted from forced marches, and supply lines were stretched. On 5 September French commander General Joseph Joffre launched a massive counter-attack along the Marne river. The Germans were exposed at a critical gap between their First and Second Armies. French and British forces drove into the gap. Famously, around 6,000 reinforcements were rushed to the front from Paris in a fleet of around 600 commandeered Parisian taxis — a small contribution but a powerful symbol of national mobilisation.

By 12 September the German army had been forced to retreat north to the Aisne river. Moltke suffered a nervous collapse and was sacked. The German government’s spokesman admitted: ‘the war is now lost’, though the fighting would in fact continue for another four years. The retreat ended the Schlieffen timetable. France had not collapsed in six weeks. Russia was already attacking in East Prussia. The Germans now faced exactly the two-front war the plan had been designed to avoid.

From mid-September each side tried to outflank the other to the north — the so-called ‘race to the sea’. By the First Battle of Ypres in late October 1914 both armies had reached the English Channel. There was nowhere left to manoeuvre. Both sides dug in. By late November the Western Front had become a continuous line of trenches running roughly 700 km from the Channel coast to the Swiss border. Movement gave way to siege. The war that was supposed to be over by Christmas would last another four years. The failure of the Schlieffen Plan therefore did not just cost Germany the campaign of 1914 — it produced the strategic deadlock that defined the rest of the war.

Key Fact

The Schlieffen Plan failed for three connected reasons: Belgian resistance at Liège cost critical days; Russia mobilised faster than expected, forcing Germany to divert troops east; and Joffre’s counter-attack at the Marne (5-12 September 1914) drove the over-extended German right wing back to the Aisne.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on the failure of the Schlieffen Plan, the strongest answers explain why each event mattered, not just what happened. A list of dates — Belgium, Marne, Aisne, trenches — will only reach the middle band. Show the causal logic: Belgian resistance bought time, which let the BEF deploy, which fed into the French line, which Joffre then exploited at the Marne. Use connectives such as ‘this delay allowed’ or ‘in consequence of which’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Schlieffen Plan was Germany’s answer to the two-front problem — defeat France in six weeks via Belgium, then turn east against Russia.
  • Belgian resistance, BEF intervention at Mons, faster-than-expected Russian mobilisation and German over-extension all combined to slow the advance.
  • Joffre’s counter-attack at the Marne (5-12 September 1914) ended the Schlieffen timetable; the resulting race to the sea produced the trench stalemate that defined the rest of the war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a despatch by French general Joseph Joffre to the French government, dated 6 September 1914, drawn from the records of the French Ministry of War.
‘Soldiers of France: at the moment when the battle on which the salvation of the country depends is about to begin, no man may look behind. Every effort must be directed at attacking and driving the enemy back. A unit which can no longer advance must hold the ground it has won at any cost and die where it stands rather than retreat.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Joffre gives for the importance of the Battle of the Marne.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• The salvation of France depended on the battle (‘the salvation of the country’).
• Every soldier must attack and drive the enemy back, not retreat.
• Holding ground was vital — units must ‘die where they stand’ rather than fall back.
• The order was meant to instil determination at the decisive moment of the campaign.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Belgian resistance, Liège forts, BEF at Mons, German overextension, Joffre’s counter-attack, Moltke’s collapse); reaches the retreat to the Aisne through a substantiated sequence.
