Indicative content:
• 4 August 1914: Germany invaded Belgium; Liège forts held longer than planned, costing critical days.
• 23 August 1914: BEF held the German advance at Mons before retreating in good order.
• Late August 1914: Russian invasion of East Prussia forced Germany to divert troops east, weakening the right wing.
• Early September 1914: German armies neared Paris; the French government fled to Bordeaux.
• 5 September 1914: Joffre counter-attacked along the Marne; a gap opened between the German First and Second Armies.
• 6-9 September 1914: French and British troops drove into the gap, supported by Parisian taxis ferrying reinforcements.
• 12 September 1914: German army retreated to the Aisne; Moltke suffered nervous collapse and was sacked.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the official war diary of British general Sir John French, commander of the BEF, dated 25 August 1914, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘The men have done magnificently at Mons. The volume and accuracy of their rifle fire shocked the Germans into thinking they faced machine guns at every point of our line. We have inflicted heavy losses, but our left flank is now exposed. Retreat is the only choice.’

Source C: An extract from a 1925 memoir by German general Alexander von Kluck, commander of the German First Army in 1914, recalling the campaign.
‘The British Expeditionary Force, small as it was, fought with a discipline I had not expected from a colonial army. At Mons and the days that followed, our timetable suffered. We could not afford four days of attrition we had not budgeted for. Yet the strategic mistake was not at Mons — it was the gap that opened between the First and Second Armies in early September.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the BEF’s contribution to the Allied campaign of 1914. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Sir John French records professional BEF rifle fire shocking the Germans; flank exposed forced retreat. Provenance: an official war diary by the BEF commander, written contemporaneously — likely candid, though shaped by the commander’s wish to record his force’s success.
Source C — Content: Kluck acknowledges British discipline cost his army four critical days. Provenance: a German general’s post-war memoir — useful as enemy testimony but written more than a decade later, with Kluck’s reputation invested in explaining the failure.
Own knowledge: The BEF was small (around 100,000) but professional; Mons (23 August) and Le Cateau (26 August) inflicted disproportionate casualties; the BEF rejoined the French line at the Marne where the gap Kluck mentions was exploited.
Judgement: B is highly useful as immediate British perspective; C is useful as German recognition but shaped by hindsight. Together they confirm the BEF’s contribution mattered out of proportion to its size.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a private letter by Helmuth von Moltke (the Younger) to his wife, dated 9 September 1914, drawn from the Moltke Family Archive.
‘I cannot bear what I see. The right wing weakens with every march. Our flanks are exposed. The French counter-attack on the Marne is a disaster from which we will not recover this campaign. Your husband, broken by what he was set to do.’

Source E: An extract from a 1915 cartoon caption in the French satirical magazine Le Rire, depicting Marshal Joffre patting the side of a Parisian taxi while Schlieffen weeps in the corner.
‘The cab driver who saved Paris. He charged the meter. Schlieffen would have charged the world.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘Moltke’s modifications to the Schlieffen Plan were the main reason for its failure in 1914.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows Moltke himself recognised that the right wing’s weakness was decisive.
• Moltke had transferred troops east to face Russia and strengthened the left wing — both at the right wing’s expense.
• Schlieffen’s deathbed warning — ‘keep the right wing strong’ — has been used to support this view (though the quotation is doubted).
• Gerhard Ritter argued Moltke effectively undid the plan.
Challenging the claim:
• Belgian resistance at Liège bought four critical days regardless of Moltke’s changes.
• BEF intervention at Mons further slowed the advance.
• Russia mobilised faster than the plan had anticipated, forcing some diversion east.
• Source E captures the symbolic role of French defence — the plan also depended on French passivity which Joffre denied it.
• Logistical limits — German supply lines were already over-extended before the Marne — would have caused trouble in any version of the plan.
Judgement: Moltke’s modifications mattered, but the plan rested on assumptions (Russian slowness, French passivity, Belgian capitulation) that were unrealistic regardless. The failure was as much structural as personal.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British War Office assessment of the Battle of the Marne, written in October 1914, drawn from the National Archives at Kew.
‘The German advance has been halted at the Marne. Three factors combined to produce this outcome: stiffened French resistance under Joffre; the timely arrival of the BEF on the Allied left; and the over-extension of the German right wing, which permitted a gap to form between the First and Second Armies. The strategic significance of the battle is that the German plan to defeat France in six weeks has been definitively frustrated.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying why the Schlieffen Plan failed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: The source identifies three causes of the Marne outcome — French resistance, BEF arrival, and German over-extension — useful evidence for a multi-factor explanation.
• Provenance: A confidential War Office assessment written within weeks of the battle — likely to express genuine professional analysis without propaganda gloss.
• Own knowledge: The factors listed match the historical record; Moltke’s nervous collapse, the gap between First and Second Armies, and the BEF’s reinforcement of the French left are well documented.
• Limitation: An October 1914 British assessment cannot draw on later evidence (German memoirs, etc.); it captures contemporary British thinking, not the full picture.

lessons.title: Trench Warfare on the Western Front
lessons.description: Trench systems, machine guns, gas and the war of attrition that dominated the Western Front from 1915.
lessons.content_html:
Why Stalemate?

By the end of 1914 a continuous line of trenches ran roughly 700 km from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border. Movement had stopped. Why? Defensive technology in 1914 was decisively stronger than offensive technology. Machine guns could fire 500 rounds a minute and could be operated by two men; barbed wire could be strung in great belts that took hours to cut; pre-registered artillery could lay down devastating barrages on any visible attack. Cavalry — the traditional arm of breakthrough — had become useless against entrenched infantry. The result was a strategic deadlock that defined the Western Front from late 1914 until the spring of 1918. Movement returned only with the combined-arms offensives that the Allies finally mastered in the Hundred Days.

Key Fact

The Western Front stalemate was the product of three combined defensive advantages: machine guns (500 rounds per minute), barbed wire belts that slowed infantry, and pre-registered artillery that could destroy attacks before they reached enemy lines. Cavalry, the traditional weapon of breakthrough, had become obsolete against entrenched defence.

Inside a Trench System

A typical British trench was a complex three-line system, not a single ditch. Front-line trenches faced the enemy across a strip of broken ground called no man’s land. Behind these came support trenches, usually 70-100 metres back, and reserve trenches further to the rear. Communication trenches connected the lines. Trenches were dug in zig-zag traverses to limit the damage from a shell exploding inside. Sandbags reinforced the parapet (front edge) and parados (rear edge). Duckboards lined the floor against the perpetual mud. Dugouts were carved into the wall for sleeping and shelter. The German army built deeper, more elaborate concrete bunkers; the British and French generally relied on lighter field fortifications, expecting (often wrongly) to advance soon.

A British infantryman’s month was structured around rotation. Roughly four to six days were spent in the front-line trench, then a similar period in the support and reserve lines, then a longer rest period further back. The day in the front line began before dawn with stand-to: every soldier on the firing step ready for an enemy attack. After dawn came rifle and trench cleaning, sentry duty, sleep in shifts, then stand-to again at dusk. Most actual fighting — raids, patrols, repair work in no man’s land — happened at night. Lice, rats, mud, ‘trench foot’ (caused by prolonged exposure to wet conditions) and the constant threat of artillery were the daily realities.

Machine Guns, Wire and Artillery

The Vickers and Maxim machine guns of 1914 could fire roughly 500 rounds per minute and required only a small crew. A handful of well-sited machine guns could pin down an entire battalion. Barbed wire was the second pillar of defence: rolls strung between iron stakes, sometimes in belts dozens of metres deep, slowed attackers and channelled them into pre-set killing zones. The third pillar was artillery. By 1916 most front-line casualties came from shells, not rifles or machine guns. Pre-registered guns could fire on map references the moment an attack began. Counter-battery fire — using sound-ranging and aerial observation — could silence enemy guns before they could intervene. The combination meant that any attack across no man’s land faced devastating, layered fire.

Poison Gas and New Weapons

Both sides searched for ways to break the deadlock. Germany released chlorine gas at Ypres in April 1915 — the first large-scale use of poison gas in modern war. Phosgene followed; mustard gas in 1917 burned skin and lungs and was the most feared. Gas caused terrible suffering but rarely produced a decisive breakthrough: prevailing winds were unreliable and gas masks improved quickly. Tanks made their debut at Flers-Courcelette on the Somme in September 1916. They were unreliable at first — many broke down before reaching enemy lines — but by Cambrai in November 1917 the British deployed nearly 400 tanks together to spectacular initial effect. Aircraft began as reconnaissance but evolved through fighters and bombers; the German Stoßtruppen (stormtroopers) of 1918 used infiltration tactics to bypass strongpoints. Each innovation chipped at the deadlock without breaking it.

A War of Attrition

When breakthrough proved impossible, both sides turned to attrition — grinding the enemy down through sustained loss. German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn explicitly chose attritional warfare at Verdun in February 1916, hoping to ‘bleed France white’. The Battle of the Somme (July-November 1916) was conceived in part as Allied pressure to relieve Verdun. The first day of the Somme — 1 July 1916 — produced 57,470 British casualties, the worst single day in the British Army’s history. Total Somme casualties on all sides exceeded one million. Attrition was therefore not a failure of generalship but a deliberate strategy: if you cannot win by movement, you win by counting.

A common belief, popularised by the BBC television series Blackadder Goes Forth and Alan Clark’s 1961 book The Donkeys, is that British generals were uncaring incompetents who hurled brave soldiers at impossible objectives. Revisionist historians — including Gary Sheffield in Forgotten Victory, John Terraine and Dan Todman — have challenged this. They point to the steep learning curve the BEF travelled: by 1918 it was using creeping artillery barrages, combined-arms tactics, accurate counter-battery fire, tanks and aircraft together. The Hundred Days offensive of August-November 1918 produced the most rapid advance the Western Front would see and was won, in large part, by the BEF. Generals were not flawless — but the caricature of incompetent butchers does not survive contact with the evidence. Strong exam answers acknowledge the popular myth and explain why it has been challenged.

Key Fact

The first day of the Battle of the Somme — 1 July 1916 — produced 57,470 British casualties, the worst single day in British military history. The five-month battle saw over one million casualties on all sides and ended with limited territorial gains, exemplifying the war of attrition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark Source Utility question on trench warfare, examiners will reward responses that distinguish between different kinds of source. A propaganda poster is highly useful for studying public opinion or government messaging, even if unreliable as a record of actual conditions. A soldier’s diary is useful for personal experience but cannot show the whole strategic picture. Always anchor your judgement to a specific question: useful for what?
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Western Front stalemate emerged because defensive technology — machine guns, barbed wire, pre-registered artillery — outmatched offensive technology, making cavalry obsolete and infantry attacks ruinously costly.
  • Trench systems were three-line networks with rotation routines, dugouts, communication trenches and zig-zag traverses; gas, tanks and aircraft chipped at but did not break the deadlock.
  • Attrition was a deliberate strategy — chosen by Falkenhayn at Verdun and reflected at the Somme — producing terrible costs but also driving the BEF’s learning curve that finally broke the line in 1918.

‘At the Front your comrades stand in mud, holding the line for England. They ask you only this: come and stand beside us. Your country needs you. Will you wait until the trenches reach Dover before you answer?’

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by British infantryman Private Ernest Cooper to his mother, dated October 1916, drawn from the Cooper Family Papers held at the Imperial War Museum.
‘Mother, do not believe what the papers say about the Front. The mud is up to our knees. Every man has trench foot and lice. The shelling is constant. We have been told tomorrow will be a great push. The men are not afraid; they are tired. Tired beyond what you can imagine at home.’

Source C: An extract from a 1928 memoir by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, recalling the Battle of the Somme of July-November 1916.
‘The Somme was a strategic necessity. The relief of Verdun, the holding of the German army to the Western Front, and the building of an experienced British army for 1917 — all required us to attack and to hold the line in attack. Casualties were grievous, but the alternative was worse.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the experience and strategy of the Battle of the Somme. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: A frontline soldier’s testimony — mud, trench foot, lice, exhaustion. Provenance: a private letter from son to mother, written contemporaneously — likely candid but limited to one section of front, and may have been written to reassure rather than fully describe.
Source C — Content: Haig defends attrition as strategically necessary. Provenance: a memoir written more than a decade later by the British commander — useful for strategic argument, but shaped by Haig’s reputational stake in defending his decisions.
Own knowledge: 1 July 1916 produced 57,470 British casualties; the Somme did relieve Verdun and inflicted heavy German losses; the BEF that fought on the Somme was largely Kitchener volunteers without prior battle experience.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the soldier’s experience but not for strategy; C is useful for strategic intent but partial in its framing. Used together they capture both ends of the chain.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a German General Staff order on infiltration tactics, dated January 1918, drawn from the captured German military records held at the Bundesarchiv-Militärarchiv, Freiburg.
‘The new offensive doctrine requires shock troops to bypass enemy strongpoints, leaving them for following echelons to reduce. Speed of penetration is decisive; an attack that halts to consume itself against a single position will achieve nothing. The objective is the enemy artillery line, not the front trench.’

Source E: An extract from a 1918 cartoon caption in the British satirical magazine Punch, depicting a British general with a chessboard before him, marked with infantry, tanks, aircraft and artillery.
‘The new game. He has learned that no piece moves alone. The Kaiser, opposite, still plays his old gambit.’

Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows German stormtrooper infiltration tactics that produced the rapid Spring Offensive gains of 1918.
• Source E captures Allied combined-arms thinking — infantry, tanks, aircraft and artillery used together — which delivered the Hundred Days.
• Creeping barrages, accurate counter-battery fire, tanks at Cambrai (1917) and Amiens (1918), aircraft for spotting and ground attack — together broke trench defences.
• Gary Sheffield’s Forgotten Victory argues the BEF’s learning curve was decisive.
Challenging the claim:
• American manpower (around two million by autumn 1918) added the weight that made breakthrough sustainable.
• German exhaustion after the failed Spring Offensive — combined with the naval blockade and home-front collapse — meant resistance was thinner.
• The Allied Generalissimo Foch coordinated the final offensives in a way that earlier years had not seen.
Judgement: tactics and technology mattered greatly, but combined with manpower advantage, German exhaustion and improved Allied coordination. New tactics broke the line; multiple factors made breaking it count.

Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British medical report on trench casualties, dated November 1916, drawn from the records of the Royal Army Medical Corps held at the National Archives at Kew.
‘Of the casualties this month, 60 per cent were caused by artillery fire, 25 per cent by machine gun and rifle fire, and 8 per cent by gas. The remaining 7 per cent reflected miscellaneous causes including disease, trench foot, and accident. The dominance of artillery confirms that the modern Western Front is principally a battle of guns.’

Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.

Indicative content:
• Content: The report shows artillery accounted for 60 per cent of casualties — useful evidence that the Western Front was dominated by guns rather than rifle or hand-to-hand combat.
• Provenance: A confidential medical report from the Royal Army Medical Corps — likely accurate, with no propaganda purpose.
• Own knowledge: This matches the historical record — by 1916 most front-line casualties came from shells, not bullets; counter-battery fire became central to operational planning.
• Limitation: One month’s data from one army does not capture full variation across the front, and trench foot/disease may be under-recorded if treated as non-battle casualties.

lessons.title: Verdun and the Somme, 1916
lessons.description: Falkenhayn's plan to bleed France white at Verdun and Britain's costly Somme offensive in 1916.
lessons.content_html:
1916: The Year of Attrition

By the end of 1915 the Western Front had become a 450-mile line of trenches stretching from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border. Neither side had broken the deadlock through manoeuvre, so both turned to attrition — trying to grind the other side into surrender by inflicting heavier losses than they could replace. 1916 produced the two most infamous battles of attrition in modern history: Verdun, fought by the French and Germans from February to December, and the Somme, fought largely by the British from July to November.

Key Fact

The Battle of Verdun opened on 21 February 1916. German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn aimed to ‘bleed France white’ by attacking a fortress city the French would have to defend at any cost. The battle ran for ten months and produced roughly 700,000 combined casualties.

Verdun: To Bleed France White

Falkenhayn picked Verdun for symbolic, not strategic, reasons. The city was ringed by French forts, sat on the River Meuse, and represented a century of French military pride. He believed that France would defend it whatever the cost, and that this stubbornness would allow German artillery to chew up French divisions one by one. The German bombardment on 21 February 1916 fired around one million shells in eight hours along an eight-mile front. Fort Douaumont, the largest of the surrounding forts, fell within four days.

General Philippe Pétain took command of the French defence. He rotated divisions through Verdun on a system known as the noria, so that no unit was destroyed completely — eventually around three quarters of the entire French army served at Verdun. He kept the city supplied via a single road, the Voie Sacrée (‘Sacred Way’), along which 6,000 lorries a day moved men, food and shells. The defiant order ‘Ils ne passeront pas’ (‘They shall not pass’) became a French national slogan.

The bleeding plan assumed German losses would stay low while French losses climbed. In practice the maths went both ways. By December 1916 the French had suffered around 377,000 casualties and the Germans 337,000 — the ratio was nearly even. The launch of the Somme offensive in July forced Germany to thin out the Verdun assault to send divisions north. French counter-attacks in October and December retook Forts Douaumont and Vaux. Falkenhayn was sacked in August 1916 and replaced by Hindenburg and Ludendorff.

The Somme: Britain’s First Mass Offensive

The Somme was originally planned as a joint Anglo-French offensive on a quiet sector to break through the German line. After Verdun began, the French contribution shrank from 40 divisions to 16 and the burden fell on Britain. The new British army — Pals battalions raised by Lord Kitchener and largely untested in major battle — would carry the attack.

A week-long preliminary bombardment fired 1.5 million shells along the German line, intended to destroy the wire and bury the defenders. It did neither effectively. Many British shells were duds, the wire was uncut in many places, and the German front line was protected by deep concrete dugouts up to 12 metres underground.

Key Fact

On 1 July 1916 — the first day of the Somme — the British army suffered around 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 dead. It remains the bloodiest day in British military history. The battle ran on for another 140 days and finally ended in mid-November.

Why the First Day Went So Wrong

Several errors compounded one another. The bombardment failed to cut the wire or destroy the German dugouts. The infantry were ordered to advance at walking pace in extended lines, weighed down with around 30 kilograms of equipment, on the assumption that resistance would be minimal. As the bombardment lifted, German machine-gunners climbed out of their dugouts and opened fire across no man’s land. The principle of creeping barrage, where shells lift forward in time with the infantry, was used in places but inconsistently coordinated.

On 15 September 1916 at Flers-Courcelette, Haig deployed the new British Mark I tank for the first time. Of the 49 sent into action only 32 made it to the start line, and most broke down or got stuck in shell craters. Even so, the few that worked drove infantry forward in places and signalled a tactical answer to the trench problem. Haig was criticised for committing the weapon early in small numbers; revisionist historians argue it was a sensible learning exercise.

Significance for 1916

By the end of November the British and French had advanced about six miles at the Somme. Total casualties were enormous: around 420,000 British, 200,000 French and 465,000 German. Yet the picture is not one of pure futility. The Somme drew German divisions away from Verdun and helped force Falkenhayn’s removal. It taught the British army hard lessons about artillery coordination, infantry tactics and air-ground cooperation that would matter in 1917 and 1918. For Germany, it accelerated the shift to a defensive strategy: in early 1917 they fell back to the heavily-fortified Hindenburg Line. The combined experience of Verdun and the Somme convinced both sides that breakthrough by infantry alone was impossible — future progress would have to come from technology, tactics and combined arms.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on 1916, examiners want you to use both sources as launch points and bring in your own contextual knowledge from across the wider period. Identify the named factor in the question (e.g. ‘poor leadership’) and weigh it against alternatives (terrain, technology, the strength of the German defensive position, the inexperience of Kitchener’s army). Reach a substantiated overall judgement — not a fence-sitting summary. Strong responses use precise figures (57,470 casualties, 1.5 million shells, six-mile advance) rather than vague impressions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Verdun (Feb–Dec 1916) was Falkenhayn’s attempt to ‘bleed France white’ at a fortress city the French would defend at any cost — it failed because German losses kept pace with French losses and the Somme forced him to divert troops.
  • The Somme (July–Nov 1916) opened with the bloodiest day in British military history because the bombardment did not cut the wire or destroy the German dugouts, and infantry walked into prepared machine-gun fire.
  • 1916 ended the idea of breakthrough by infantry alone — both sides moved towards combined arms (tanks, creeping barrage, air-ground cooperation) and Germany withdrew to the Hindenburg Line for 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the diary of British infantryman Private Cyril Tyler of the Sherwood Foresters, written in his trench notebook on the night of 1 July 1916.
‘We went over at half past seven. The wire was not cut where we crossed and the men piled up against it. The Hun guns started before we had gone twenty yards and we could see they were not in the least shaken by our shells. We lost the company commander and most of the officers in the first minute.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons the first-day Somme attack failed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Uncut barbed wire trapped attackers (‘the wire was not cut… the men piled up against it’).
• The British bombardment failed to suppress the German defenders (‘not in the least shaken by our shells’).
• German machine guns opened fire almost immediately (‘the Hun guns started before we had gone twenty yards’).
• The loss of officers in the opening minute disrupted command on the spot.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum written by German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn to Kaiser Wilhelm II in December 1915, drawn from German military archives published after the war.
‘France has reached the limit of what she can endure. If we choose a sector she must defend at all costs, the French army will bleed itself to death within range of our guns whether or not we take the position. Verdun, with its forts and history, is such a sector.’

Source C: An extract from a despatch by French general Robert Nivelle in October 1916, sent to the French High Command after the recapture of Fort Douaumont.
‘Eight months of attack have cost the enemy as dearly as they have cost us. Our losses are heavy, but our soldiers are not broken. The German army has spent itself before our guns no less than we have spent ourselves before theirs. They shall not pass.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Battle of Verdun. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: shows Falkenhayn’s explicit reasoning that Verdun was chosen because France would have to defend it. Provenance: a strategic memo to the Kaiser; intended to justify a plan, so likely to overstate confidence. Own knowledge: French final losses (~377,000) and German (~337,000) made the bleeding plan a near-even exchange, undermining the strategy.
Source C — Content: a French claim that Verdun has cost Germany as much as France. Provenance: an official despatch after the recapture of Douaumont, intended to boost morale; may exaggerate German exhaustion. Own knowledge: the rotation of divisions through the noria and the Voie Sacrée supply road kept France in the fight; the Somme also drew German troops away.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German strategic thinking but partial; C is useful as contemporary French reaction but reflects propaganda value. Together they show the gap between Falkenhayn’s plan and its actual outcome.

Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 24 June 1916: a seven-day British bombardment fired 1.5 million shells; many were duds, the wire was largely uncut, and German dugouts survived.
• 1 July 1916: at 7.30am infantry advanced in extended lines; ~57,470 casualties on the first day, including 19,240 dead.
• July–August: smaller-scale attacks (Mametz Wood, High Wood, Pozières) ground forward at heavy cost.
• 15 September 1916: tanks deployed for the first time at Flers-Courcelette; mechanically unreliable but pointed towards combined-arms tactics.
• October–November: rain turned the battlefield to mud; the offensive halted in mid-November after a six-mile advance.
• Outcome: ~420,000 British, 200,000 French and 465,000 German casualties; Germany withdrew in early 1917 to the Hindenburg Line.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from a despatch by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, sent to the British War Cabinet on 23 December 1916 and later published in The London Gazette.
‘The objects with which we entered the battle on 1 July were three: to relieve the pressure on Verdun, to assist our Allies in the other theatres, and to wear down the strength of the enemy in the field. All these were achieved.’

Source E: An extract from a 1917 article by British war correspondent Philip Gibbs in The Daily Chronicle, reflecting on the Somme campaign.
‘Six miles of mud has been bought at a price our country will count for a generation. The men did everything that was asked of them. The plan asked too much.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The Battle of the Somme was a costly failure that achieved very little.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source E captures public reaction to enormous cost (‘six miles of mud’) for limited ground gained.
• First-day casualties of ~57,470 and total British losses of ~420,000 dwarfed the territorial advance.
• Many tactical errors on 1 July: walking-pace advance, uncut wire, surviving German dugouts.
Challenging the claim:
• Source D states three strategic aims — relieving Verdun, supporting allies, wearing down Germany — and modern scholarship accepts the first and third were partly met.
• The Somme drew German divisions north and contributed to Falkenhayn’s sacking in August 1916.
• Tactical lessons (creeping barrage, tank co-operation, artillery coordination, sound-ranging) carried into 1917 and 1918.
• Germany was forced into the defensive Hindenburg Line withdrawal in early 1917.
Provenance points: Haig writes officially to defend his command, so Source D may overstate success; Gibbs writes for a public audience after censorship constraints lifted, so Source E reflects a developing critical narrative. Both partial in different directions.
Judgement: failure to break through is fair, but ‘achieved very little’ understates the strategic and tactical contribution of the campaign to the wider war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the war diary of German staff officer Captain Friedrich von Lossberg, recording observations after touring the Somme front line in late September 1916. The diary is held in the German Federal Military Archives.
‘The English artillery is no longer the chaotic curtain of last year. Their barrage now moves with the infantry as one body. Our forward dugouts give less protection than before. The men in the line speak of the new motor-vehicles — the tanks — with a fear we have not yet learned to answer.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying tactical change at the Somme in 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: the source records a German recognition that British creeping barrage was working in 1916 — useful evidence that tactical learning was happening even within a costly campaign.
• Content: it captures the early psychological impact of tanks on German troops, supporting the view that Flers-Courcelette mattered beyond the breakdowns.
• Provenance: a contemporary war diary by a senior staff officer touring the line is well-placed to assess tactical change; less likely to be sanitised for public consumption than a press article.
• Own knowledge: this matches subsequent German moves — the Hindenburg Line withdrawal in early 1917 and the development of elastic defence-in-depth in response to British artillery effectiveness.
• Limitation worth noting: a single staff officer’s observations are not the same as system-wide German practice, so the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive.

lessons.title: Passchendaele and the Tactical Learning Curve
lessons.description: Third Ypres in the mud of 1917 and the BEF's tactical learning curve in tanks and combined arms.
lessons.content_html:
A Third Battle at Ypres

After the slaughter of 1916, Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig wanted a 1917 offensive that could break out of the Ypres salient, drive towards the Belgian coast, and capture the U-boat bases at Ostend and Zeebrugge. The result became known officially as the Third Battle of Ypres, but to the soldiers and the public as Passchendaele, after the small Flemish village finally captured in November.

Key Fact

The Third Battle of Ypres ran from 31 July to 10 November 1917. Haig aimed to break out of the salient, capture the Belgian coast and force a German collapse. After three months of mud and rain the Allies advanced about five miles for around 275,000 British and Empire casualties and roughly 220,000 German.

The Mud of Flanders

The opening preparation was the largest Allied bombardment yet seen — over four million shells fired in two weeks, ten times the weight delivered before the Somme. The bombardment shattered the drainage system that had kept the Flanders plain workable, and the wettest August in thirty years turned the broken ground into liquid mud. Tanks could not move. Wounded men drowned in shell holes. Each step forward had to be reclaimed metre by metre.

Three commanders led the British effort. General Sir Hubert Gough, an aggressive cavalry officer, was meant to break out fast; he could not. Haig replaced him with General Sir Herbert Plumer, a careful planner who had captured the Messines Ridge in June 1917 by detonating 19 huge mines under the German line — an explosion heard in London. Plumer’s methodical bite and hold approach — small advances secured by overwhelming artillery before the next move — produced the only consistent gains of the campaign at Menin Road, Polygon Wood and Broodseinde.

The Flanders plain was below sea level in places and only farmable because of three centuries of drainage ditches and pumps. The bombardment ground these to powder. Shell craters filled with rainwater within hours, then linked into chains of pools. Mud caked rifles, swallowed boots, and made shells that did not detonate vanish into the soft earth. Some historians argue Haig should have called off the offensive when the rain began — others note the strategic pressure to keep Germany occupied while the French army recovered from the mutinies that followed General Nivelle’s catastrophic April 1917 offensive.

The BEF’s Quiet Learning Curve

The image of static, futile slaughter has dominated public memory of the Western Front. Yet between 1915 and 1917 the British Expeditionary Force underwent a remarkable transformation. By Passchendaele the BEF was using tactics that simply did not exist on the Somme. Sound-ranging located German batteries from the noise of their own guns and silenced them before infantry attacked. Aerial photography produced detailed trench maps that artillery could fire on without giving away the attack by registering shots in advance.

Infantry tactics changed too. Battalions were reorganised into platoons combining riflemen, bombers, Lewis-gunners and rifle-grenadiers, so that small groups could fight forward against enemy strongpoints. The creeping barrage became more accurate, with shells lifting at a tighter walking pace. Tanks, although hopeless in the Flanders mud, proved their potential at Cambrai on 20 November 1917, when 476 tanks broke the Hindenburg Line on a six-mile front before German counter-attacks recovered most of the ground.

Key Fact

By the end of 1917 the BEF was deploying combined-arms tactics: predicted artillery fire, sound-ranging, aerial reconnaissance, platoon-level infantry organisation, mass tank attacks (Cambrai, 20 November) and a more accurate creeping barrage. The tools that would win the Hundred Days in 1918 were already in place.

Lions Led By Donkeys?

The verdict that brave British soldiers were ‘lions led by donkeys’ was popularised by Alan Clark’s 1961 book The Donkeys and reinforced by the 1989 BBC comedy Blackadder Goes Forth. Modern revisionist scholarship — led by historians such as Gary Sheffield, Peter Simkins and Dan Todman — has challenged this picture. They point to the BEF’s learning curve, to operational successes such as Messines and Cambrai, and to the war-winning advances of August–November 1918.

Critics highlight Haig’s persistence with attacks at Passchendaele after the rains broke and his apparent indifference to casualty figures. Defenders point to the strategic pressure to relieve French mutinies, the absence of any tactical alternative for breaking trench warfare in 1917, and the eventual victories he commanded in 1918. The most balanced verdict is that Haig was neither the cartoon donkey of Blackadder nor a flawless commander — he led an army through a learning process that, by 1918, had produced the most effective fighting force in the world.

Significance of 1917

Passchendaele did not break out to the coast. Yet by holding the salient and absorbing German divisions through autumn 1917, it kept the pressure on a Germany that was about to gain reinforcements from Russia’s collapse on the Eastern Front. Cambrai showed the world that mass tanks, surprise and combined arms could break the trench system. The hard infantry lessons of 1915–1917 produced an army that, despite the disaster of Passchendaele’s casualty list, would carry the Allies to victory the following year.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on the BEF’s tactical learning curve, build a chain of three or four linked developments. Start with the Somme’s lessons (uncut wire, walking-pace advance, broken artillery coordination), then move through Messines (mines), Plumer’s ‘bite and hold’, sound-ranging and predicted fire, and end at Cambrai. Use connectives such as ‘this revealed’, ‘in response’, ‘by 1917’. Avoid first-person voice or diary-entry framing — examiners flag this as a recurring issue that prevents top marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Passchendaele (Third Ypres, 31 July–10 November 1917) cost around 275,000 British and Empire casualties for an advance of about five miles, in mud created by the Allied bombardment and the wettest August in thirty years.
  • By 1917 the BEF was using combined arms — sound-ranging, predicted fire, platoon tactics, accurate creeping barrage, mass tanks at Cambrai — that did not exist on the Somme.
  • The ‘lions led by donkeys’ verdict has been challenged by revisionist historians who point to a real learning curve, even if Haig’s judgement at Passchendaele itself remains disputed.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the diary of Australian Sergeant Walter Downing of the 5th Brigade AIF, written near Broodseinde in October 1917 and held in the Australian War Memorial archive.
‘The shell fire turned the Flanders fields into a swamp. Men slid into shell holes filled to the brim and could not be pulled out. Yet our guns kept walking forward in front of us at the proper pace, and where the mud allowed, we walked behind them as we had been trained.’

Using Source A, identify two features of fighting at Passchendaele in autumn 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct features drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant features from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear feature; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific features.

Indicative content:
• The battlefield had become a swamp from sustained shellfire (‘swamp… shell holes filled to the brim’).
• Soldiers drowned or could not be retrieved from flooded craters (‘could not be pulled out’).
• A creeping barrage was being used to support the infantry advance (‘our guns kept walking forward… at the proper pace’).
• Infantry were trained to advance in coordination with artillery (‘we walked behind them as we had been trained’).

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the British Expeditionary Force’s tactics evolved between the first day of the Somme on 1 July 1916 and the Battle of Cambrai on 20 November 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more developments as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Somme errors, Messines mines, Plumer’s bite and hold, sound-ranging, Cambrai); reaches Cambrai through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked developments with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant developments listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between developments.

Indicative content:
• 1 July 1916: catastrophic first-day Somme losses revealed that walking-pace advance into uncut wire and surviving German dugouts was unworkable.
• Late 1916: tanks deployed at Flers-Courcelette (15 September) showed potential despite mechanical failure.
• Early 1917: Germany withdrew to the Hindenburg Line; the BEF reorganised infantry into platoons of riflemen, bombers, Lewis-gunners and rifle-grenadiers.
• 7 June 1917: 19 mines detonated under the Messines Ridge, capturing the position cleanly with low losses — the explosion was heard in London.
• Summer 1917: General Plumer’s ‘bite and hold’ method took Menin Road, Polygon Wood and Broodseinde with overwhelming artillery support.
• 20 November 1917: 476 tanks broke the Hindenburg Line on a six-mile front at Cambrai, demonstrating mass-tank surprise attack as a tactical answer to trench warfare.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by General Sir Hubert Gough to GHQ in late August 1917, drawn from the British official history of the war.
‘The terrain is no longer practicable for the rapid breakthrough that was originally planned. The drainage of the Flanders plain is destroyed, the rains continue, and our tanks cannot move. To press on now in the same form would be to send men into a marsh.’

Source C: An extract from a War Cabinet memorandum by Field Marshal Haig, dated October 1917, recording the strategic case for continuing the offensive.
‘The French army is recovering from severe disturbance and cannot lead a major offensive this year. Russia is a broken reed; the Eastern Front will release fresh German divisions. We must keep the German forces fixed in Flanders. To break off our attack would invite catastrophe in 1918.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the decision to continue the Passchendaele offensive. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Gough acknowledges the terrain is no longer suitable for breakthrough. Provenance: a frontline army commander writing internally to GHQ; likely to give a candid operational picture, though he may also be defending his early lack of progress. Own knowledge: Haig replaced Gough with the more methodical Plumer in late August/September 1917, suggesting agreement with the operational picture.
Source C — Content: Haig argues continued attack is needed because of French mutiny recovery and the looming German reinforcement from Russia. Provenance: a senior commander writing to government; intended to justify continued offensive, so likely to overstate strategic necessity. Own knowledge: General Nivelle’s April offensive had triggered widespread French army mutinies; the Bolshevik seizure of power on 7 November 1917 confirmed that German troops would soon move west.
Judgement: B is useful for the operational reality; C is useful for strategic reasoning but partial — a defence of an unpopular decision. Together they show the gap between local conditions and high-command priorities.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from Alan Clark’s book The Donkeys, published in 1961, describing British generalship on the Western Front.
‘Brave men in the lines, blunderers in the chateaux. The British soldier walked uphill into machine guns because his commanders had no other tactical idea, and the casualty lists tell the story.’

Source E: An extract from a 2002 article by historian Gary Sheffield in History Today on the BEF’s tactical evolution.
‘Between 1915 and 1918 the British army was transformed. Sound-ranging, predicted fire, platoon tactics, mass tanks and combined arms were forged in the trenches. By August 1918 the BEF was the most effective fighting force in the world.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘British generals were incompetent and the soldiers paid the price.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D voices the well-known critical tradition; first-day Somme casualties (~57,470) and Passchendaele (~275,000) lend weight to the cost in lives.
• Tactical persistence with attacks after rain broke at Passchendaele suggests poor judgement.
• Plumer’s removal of Gough only after weeks of fruitless attack indicates command failures could be slow to correct.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E represents revisionist scholarship — Sheffield, Simkins, Todman — pointing to a genuine learning curve.
• Specific operational successes: Messines (June 1917) with 19 mines, Plumer’s bite-and-hold offensives, Cambrai’s mass tank attack (Nov 1917), the Hundred Days (Aug–Nov 1918).
• Generals operated under unprecedented strategic pressure (French mutinies, Russian collapse) without an existing template for breaking trench deadlock.
Provenance points: Clark wrote in 1961 with cultural and political motives that shaped his framing; Sheffield writes within a peer-reviewed academic tradition with later access to operational records.
Judgement: ‘incompetent’ is too strong; British generalship was uneven and made costly errors but presided over a tactical transformation that won the war by 1918.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by General Sir Herbert Plumer to his wife, dated 8 October 1917 and held in the Imperial War Museums archive.
‘Bite and hold has gained us Menin Road, Polygon Wood, and now Broodseinde. The barrage moves at the proper rate; the men keep behind it; we take the ground we can hold and stop. We do not chase glory across mud we cannot move guns over. The men deserve nothing less.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying British tactics in 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: the source records Plumer’s ‘bite and hold’ doctrine in his own words and names three specific successes (Menin Road, Polygon Wood, Broodseinde) — useful primary evidence of how the tactic was framed.
• Content: it shows artillery–infantry coordination (‘the barrage moves at the proper rate; the men keep behind it’) — supports the broader claim of tactical sophistication by 1917.
• Provenance: a private letter from the commander himself to his wife, less likely to be performative than a public despatch; well-placed to capture his thinking.
• Own knowledge: this matches the chronology — bite-and-hold replaced Gough’s push for rapid breakthrough after the early August setbacks; the same approach would extend in 1918.
• Limitation: a private letter selects what to share with a family member, so absences (e.g. mounting casualties) do not mean the writer was unaware of them.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the events of the Third Battle of Ypres between the opening bombardment in mid-July 1917 and the capture of Passchendaele village in November 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Messines, opening 31 July, Plumer takeover, capture of village 6/10 November); reaches the close of the battle through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 7 June 1917: Messines Ridge captured cleanly when 19 mines were detonated under the German line — the explosion heard in London.
• Mid-July 1917: a 14-day Allied bombardment fired over four million shells, destroying the Flanders drainage system.
• 31 July 1917: Third Ypres opened under Gough; rapid breakthrough was meant to drive towards Belgian U-boat ports but stalled in worsening rain.
• Late August 1917: Haig replaced Gough with Plumer, who introduced ‘bite and hold’.
• Sept–Oct 1917: Plumer’s carefully prepared advances took Menin Road (20 Sept), Polygon Wood (26 Sept) and Broodseinde (4 Oct).
• 6 November 1917: Canadian troops captured Passchendaele village; the offensive was halted by 10 November after roughly five miles of advance for around 275,000 British and Empire casualties.

lessons.title: The Wider War: Gallipoli and Other Fronts
lessons.description: Britain's Dardanelles gamble, ANZAC at Anzac Cove and the wider war on other fronts.
lessons.content_html:
Trying to Break the Deadlock Somewhere Else

By the end of 1914 the Western Front was a stalemate from the Channel to Switzerland. The British Cabinet split into two groups. The ‘Westerners’, including Field Marshal Sir John French and senior generals, argued that Germany could only be defeated on the Western Front. The Easterners, led by First Lord of the Admiralty Winston Churchill, argued that the deadlock could be broken by knocking out one of Germany’s allies somewhere else. Their main target was the Ottoman Empire, which had entered the war on the German side in November 1914.

Key Fact

The Gallipoli campaign opened with a naval attack on 19 February 1915 and the major land landings on 25 April 1915. British, French, Australian, New Zealand and Indian troops fought to seize the Dardanelles straits, knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea route to Russia. The campaign was abandoned in January 1916 after roughly 250,000 Allied casualties.

The Strategic Logic

Capturing the Dardanelles would have allowed Allied ships to reach Constantinople. The aims were ambitious. First, the Ottoman government would be forced to surrender, freeing British troops fighting in Mesopotamia and Palestine. Second, a sea route would open through the Black Sea to Russia, which was desperate for shells and rifles. Third, the success might bring neutral Bulgaria, Greece and Romania into the war on the Allied side. Fourth, it would offer an alternative to head-on attacks in France. Churchill championed the operation; the War Council approved it in January 1915.

The first attempt was naval. On 18 March 1915 a fleet of British and French battleships tried to force the straits by gunfire alone. They were stopped by Turkish mines. Three battleships sank and three more were heavily damaged. The naval commander wanted to try again the next day, but the operation was suspended. Land troops would now have to clear the peninsula by foot.

The five-week gap between the failed naval attack and the land landings on 25 April gave the Ottomans time to prepare. German general Liman von Sanders organised the defence and his subordinate, Mustafa Kemal (later Atatürk), led the troops who pinned the ANZACs to the beaches. The British and French landed at Cape Helles in the south. The Australians and New Zealanders — the ANZAC — landed about a mile north of their intended beach at what became known as Anzac Cove. Steep cliffs stopped any rapid advance. Within days the front had become a smaller version of the Western Front: trenches, machine guns, no man’s land.

Why Gallipoli Failed

Several factors combined. Allied intelligence about Ottoman strength was poor. The decision to use a naval attack first removed all surprise from the later land landing. The terrain was vertical and waterless and the August heat was crippling. Disease, especially dysentery and typhoid, took as many men out of the line as wounds. Ottoman troops, fighting on home soil and led by capable commanders, fought far harder than Allied planners had assumed. By the time British and Empire reinforcements landed at Suvla Bay in August 1915, the Ottomans held the high ground in strength. Evacuation began in December 1915 and was completed in January 1916 — the cleanest, least bloody phase of the campaign. Allied casualties reached around 250,000, including roughly 26,000 ANZACs (8,700 Australian and 2,700 New Zealand dead). Churchill resigned from the Admiralty in May 1915 and went to fight on the Western Front.

Key Fact

Gallipoli failed for four main reasons: poor intelligence on Ottoman strength; loss of surprise after the failed naval attack on 18 March 1915; difficult terrain and disease; and skilled Ottoman defence under Mustafa Kemal and Liman von Sanders. Total Allied casualties reached around 250,000 by the January 1916 evacuation.

The Eastern Front

While the Western Front froze into trenches, the Eastern Front remained mobile. Russia had mobilised faster than Germany expected and invaded East Prussia in August 1914. German victories at Tannenberg (26–30 August 1914) and the Masurian Lakes (September 1914) destroyed two Russian armies; together they cost Russia around 250,000 casualties. The German commanders Hindenburg and Ludendorff became national heroes. Yet Russia recovered and, under General Brusilov, launched the most successful Eastern offensive of the war in summer 1916, capturing 400,000 Austrian prisoners and forcing Germany to send divisions east. The cost was huge — around a million Russian casualties — and the defeats and food shortages that followed undermined Tsar Nicholas II’s government and contributed to the February and October revolutions of 1917.

Italy joined the war on the Allied side in May 1915 after the Treaty of London promised territorial gains. The Italian army fought eleven battles along the River Isonzo against Austria-Hungary at terrible cost. The catastrophic Italian defeat at Caporetto in October–November 1917 saw Austrian and German troops, using new stormtrooper tactics, advance roughly 100 kilometres and capture around 275,000 Italian prisoners. British and French divisions had to be rushed south to stabilise the line.

Significance of the Wider War

The wider campaigns matter for two reasons. First, they show that the war was not only a Western Front war: between 1914 and 1918 fighting consumed the Eastern Front, the Italian Front, the Middle East, Africa, and the world’s oceans. Second, the failures and the costs forced lessons. Gallipoli ended the dream that the war could be ended through a clever side-attack and convinced British strategists that the main effort had to remain in France. The Eastern Front’s collapse in 1917 freed German divisions for the 1918 Spring Offensive in the west. Caporetto demonstrated that combined-arms infiltration tactics could break trench warfare — Germany would use the same approach against the British in March 1918.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Source Utility question on Gallipoli, examiner reports flag that students who only weigh provenance (‘this is biased so not useful’) cap themselves at the lower bands. Top-band answers integrate three things for each source: content (what the source actually says), provenance (who made it, when, why) and own contextual knowledge (specific facts you bring — 18 March naval failure, 25 April landings, Mustafa Kemal, ~250,000 casualties). Always reach a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gallipoli (Feb 1915–Jan 1916) was the ‘Easterners’’ attempt to break the deadlock by knocking out the Ottoman Empire and opening a sea route to Russia — it failed because of lost surprise, terrain, disease and skilled Turkish defence.
  • The Eastern Front saw mobile warfare and huge Russian losses (Tannenberg 1914, Brusilov Offensive 1916), eventually contributing to the Russian revolutions of 1917.
  • The wider war shaped Western Front strategy: Gallipoli ended faith in side-attacks, the Eastern Front’s collapse freed German divisions for 1918, and Caporetto previewed stormtrooper tactics.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the official war diary of an Australian battalion at Anzac Cove, written on the night of 25 April 1915 and held in the Australian War Memorial archive.
‘We have been ashore since dawn. The cliffs above the beach are held in strength and our advance has not reached its objectives. The cove was not the beach we were directed towards. Casualties heavy and no clear position from which to organise the next attempt.’

Using Source A, identify two features of the Anzac Cove landing on 25 April 1915.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct features drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant features from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear feature; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific features.

Indicative content:
• The cliffs above the beach were defended in strength (‘the cliffs above the beach are held in strength’).
• Initial objectives were not reached (‘our advance has not reached its objectives’).
• Troops landed at the wrong beach (‘the cove was not the beach we were directed towards’).
• Casualties were heavy from the first day (‘casualties heavy and no clear position’).

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum written by Winston Churchill to the British War Council in January 1915, drawn from the records of the Cabinet Office.
‘Are we to admit that there is no other way of winning the war than by sending fresh armies to slaughter on the Western Front? The Dardanelles offers the only short cut. Force the straits, and Constantinople falls. The Black Sea opens to Russia, the Balkan states join us, and the German alliance crumbles.’

Source C: An extract from a despatch by Sir Ian Hamilton, the British commander at Gallipoli, sent to Lord Kitchener in August 1915 from the peninsula.
‘The terrain is more terrible than any of our advisers anticipated. The Turk fights with skill and courage on his own ground. Disease takes as many men as the rifle. We need fresh divisions, fresh water, and a clearer plan, or we cannot break out of the beachhead.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Gallipoli campaign. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: lays out Churchill’s strategic case for the Dardanelles. Provenance: a memorandum by the operation’s leading champion to the body that would approve it; clearly intended to persuade and likely to overstate prospects. Own knowledge: the failed naval attack on 18 March 1915 stopped the strategic vision in its tracks; only four neutral states ever joined the Allies and not because of the Dardanelles.
Source C — Content: gives a frontline assessment of why the campaign was failing — terrain, Ottoman skill, disease. Provenance: a despatch from the British commander to the Secretary of State for War; well-placed to assess operational reality but also defending his own conduct. Own knowledge: Ottoman defence under Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal exploited the high ground; Suvla Bay landings in August failed to break out; evacuation completed January 1916 with ~250,000 Allied casualties.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the strategic vision but partial; C is useful for operational realities but written by a commander defending his record. Together they show why the side-attack idea collapsed.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Gallipoli campaign developed from the naval attack in February 1915 to the final evacuation in January 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (19 Feb naval bombardment, 18 March, 25 April, Suvla Bay, evacuation Dec 1915–Jan 1916); reaches the close of the campaign through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 19 February 1915: opening Anglo-French naval bombardment of the Dardanelles forts.
• 18 March 1915: full naval assault halted by Turkish mines; three Allied battleships sank.
• Five-week pause allowed Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal to organise the Ottoman defence.
• 25 April 1915: land landings at Cape Helles (British/French) and Anzac Cove (ANZACs); steep cliffs and prepared defenders pinned the attack to the beaches.
• August 1915: Suvla Bay landings sought to break out but were blocked by Ottoman positions on the high ground; disease (dysentery, typhoid) crippled the force.
• December 1915–January 1916: cleanly executed evacuation removed troops with low casualties; total Allied casualties reached around 250,000.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from a 1923 memoir by Lord Hankey, secretary to the British War Council during the planning of Gallipoli.
‘The Dardanelles plan was strategically sound and operationally botched. Speed and surprise were essential and both were thrown away. Had we landed in February without warning the Turks, Constantinople might have fallen.’

Source E: An extract from a 1956 article by historian Robert Rhodes James in The English Historical Review.
‘The premise that the Ottoman Empire would collapse with the fall of Constantinople was untested optimism. The terrain at Gallipoli would have favoured defenders even with surprise, and the absence of an army-navy command structure would have produced muddle in any scenario.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘Gallipoli was a strategically sound plan ruined by poor execution.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D defends the strategic logic and blames execution — the failed naval-first approach handed five weeks’ preparation to the Ottomans.
• Specific operational errors: poor intelligence on Ottoman strength; landing at the wrong beach at Anzac Cove; failure to exploit Suvla Bay surprise in August.
• Churchill’s political championing of a difficult plan was followed by inconsistent military command (Hamilton replaced; piecemeal reinforcement).
Challenging the claim:
• Source E argues the strategic premise itself was flawed — Constantinople’s fall might not have collapsed the Ottoman Empire; the Dardanelles defenders would have held even with surprise.
• Terrain (steep cliffs, no fresh water, narrow beaches) was structurally hostile.
• Disease (dysentery, typhoid) and the August heat made operations unsustainable regardless of plan.
• Ottoman troops under Mustafa Kemal and Liman von Sanders were better than Allied planners assumed.
Provenance points: Hankey was an insider in 1923 with reputational interest in defending the strategic concept; Rhodes James writes within an academic tradition with later access to Turkish records.
Judgement: ‘sound plan ruined by execution’ overstates the strategic logic; the operation combined contestable strategic premises with specific operational failures.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a memoir by Russian general Aleksei Brusilov, written in the 1920s and published in English translation as A Soldier’s Notebook.
‘In June 1916 my four armies broke the Austrian line on a 350-kilometre front. We took prisoners by the hundreds of thousands. Yet the Tsar’s government failed to send the reserves required to exploit the breach, and within weeks German divisions arrived from France to stiffen the line. Our victory dissolved into bleeding.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the Eastern Front in 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: provides a commander’s account of the Brusilov Offensive — useful evidence of the scale of the initial breakthrough on a 350-km front.
• Content: identifies a key reason the offensive was not exploited — failure of the Tsarist government to provide reserves; supports the argument that Russian state weakness, not just military failure, undermined the war effort.
• Provenance: written by the commanding general himself, well-placed to recall the operational shape; published in the 1920s after Russian Revolution, so likely to frame the Tsarist regime critically.
• Own knowledge: matches the historical record — roughly 400,000 Austrian prisoners taken; Russian casualties around one million; Germans had to send divisions east, easing pressure on the Western Front. The strain on the Tsarist regime fed into the 1917 revolutions.
• Limitation: a commander’s self-account may underplay any operational shortcomings on his own side.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the major events on the Eastern Front between Russia’s mobilisation in August 1914 and the Brusilov Offensive of summer 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Tannenberg, Masurian Lakes, Brusilov Offensive); reaches summer 1916 through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• August 1914: Russia mobilised faster than Germany expected and invaded East Prussia, drawing German troops from the Western Front.
• 26–30 August 1914: Battle of Tannenberg destroyed the Russian Second Army; Hindenburg and Ludendorff emerged as German national heroes.
• September 1914: Battle of the Masurian Lakes drove Russia out of East Prussia; combined Tannenberg and Masurian Lakes losses ~250,000.
• 1915: German and Austro-Hungarian advance pushed Russia out of Poland; Tsar Nicholas II personally took command of the army, tying him directly to the war’s reverses.
• Summer 1916: General Brusilov’s offensive broke the Austro-Hungarian line on a 350-km front; 400,000 Austrian prisoners taken; Germany forced to send divisions east, easing pressure on Verdun and the Somme.
• Cost: roughly one million Russian casualties; the strain accelerated revolutionary pressures that broke the Tsarist regime in 1917.
