lessons.title: The War at Sea: Jutland, U-boats and Convoys
lessons.description: Jellicoe versus Scheer at Jutland, the U-boat threat to Britain and the convoy system.
lessons.content_html:
A War on the Sea Lanes

In 1914 Britain was an island fed by ships. Around 60% of its food and almost all its raw materials came by sea. Germany had spent twenty years building a fleet to challenge British naval supremacy under Admiral Tirpitz’s programme. Yet for most of the war the German High Seas Fleet stayed in port. Britain’s strategy was to use its much larger Grand Fleet, based at Scapa Flow in Orkney, to impose a distant blockade. The blockade slowly cut Germany off from food and raw materials and would by 1918 contribute decisively to internal collapse.

Key Fact

The Battle of Jutland was fought on 31 May–1 June 1916 in the North Sea. Admiral Sir John Jellicoe commanded the British Grand Fleet; Admiral Reinhard Scheer commanded the German High Seas Fleet. Britain lost 14 ships and 6,094 men; Germany lost 11 ships and 2,551 men. After Jutland the German fleet rarely left port.

Jutland: The Only Big Fleet Action

Jutland was the only major fleet engagement of the war. Scheer hoped to lure part of the British fleet into a trap and destroy it before the larger Grand Fleet could intervene. He sent Vice-Admiral Hipper’s battlecruiser squadron south to draw out British battlecruisers under Vice-Admiral Beatty. Beatty took the bait and pursued; Scheer’s battleships then appeared. But Jellicoe with the main Grand Fleet was right behind Beatty — Scheer found the trap reversed against him.

The fighting was confused. Visibility was poor, signalling broke down, and Beatty’s battlecruisers proved tragically vulnerable: HMS Indefatigable, Queen Mary and Invincible all blew up when shells reached their magazines, killing more than 3,000 men. Beatty famously remarked, ‘There seems to be something wrong with our bloody ships today.’ Twice Scheer turned away under cover of destroyer smoke and torpedo runs to avoid the British battle line, and slipped home overnight. Jellicoe declined to pursue at night, knowing that a single torpedo hit on the British flagship could change the strategic balance of the war.

Germany claimed a tactical victory because it had sunk more British tonnage and lost fewer ships and men. Britain claimed strategic victory because the German High Seas Fleet returned to harbour and barely ventured out again. Winston Churchill later wrote that Jellicoe was ‘the only man on either side who could have lost the war in an afternoon’ — meaning the loss of the Grand Fleet would have ended British control of the sea, and with it Britain’s blockade and food supply. By that yardstick, Jutland was a clear British strategic victory: the blockade tightened and Germany would now turn to a different naval weapon.

U-boats and Britain’s Lifeline

Locked out of surface combat, Germany turned to the U-boat. Submarines could slip past the blockade and attack merchant shipping in the Atlantic. There was, however, a legal problem. The 1909 Declaration of London required warships stopping a merchant vessel to give the crew time to abandon ship before sinking it — the so-called ‘cruiser rules’. A submarine that surfaced to do this lost its only advantage: stealth.

Germany twice tried unrestricted submarine warfare. The first attempt began in February 1915 and produced the most famous incident: on 7 May 1915 the U-20 sank the Cunard liner RMS Lusitania off the southern coast of Ireland, killing 1,198 passengers, including 128 American citizens. American outrage forced Germany to back off in late 1915. The second attempt began on 1 February 1917 and was a deliberate gamble: Germany calculated that knocking Britain out of the war by starvation in six months was worth provoking the United States into joining the war late.

Key Fact

Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917. April 1917 was the worst month for British shipping — 881,000 tons of merchant shipping sunk. Britain was estimated to have around six weeks of food left. The convoy system, introduced from May 1917, transformed the war at sea.

The Convoy System

The Royal Navy was initially against convoying merchant ships. Senior admirals argued that warships were better used hunting U-boats than escorting traders, and that gathering merchantmen into groups would simply hand the U-boats bigger targets. Junior officers and David Lloyd George disagreed. The first experimental convoy from Gibraltar to Britain in May 1917 lost no ships. The system was rolled out across the Atlantic over the summer.

Convoying worked because it inverted the U-boat’s problem. The ocean is large; merchant ships scattered through it gave U-boats targets in many places. A convoy concentrated those targets into a small area surrounded by destroyers, depth charges and (later) air patrols. To attack a convoy, a U-boat had to find one in the first place — a much harder needle in a much bigger haystack — and then survive the escort. The combination of convoying with depth charges (a type of underwater bomb), hydrophone listening gear and aircraft cut shipping losses dramatically. By the end of 1917 monthly losses had fallen by more than half. Around 5,000 Allied merchant ships were sunk over the war, but by 1918 the U-boat threat was contained.

The British blockade tightened year by year. In the ‘Turnip Winter’ of 1916–17, German civilians were reduced to substituting turnips for almost every staple. By 1918 around 750,000 German civilians had died from blockade-related malnutrition and disease, according to a German government commission of inquiry after the war. The blockade did not directly stop the German army in 1918, but it broke the will of the home front: the Kiel naval mutiny of October 1918 began among hungry sailors ordered to make a final suicidal sortie. The contribution of the blockade to German defeat is hard to overstate — and Jutland made it possible by keeping the High Seas Fleet bottled up.

Significance

The war at sea had three decisive effects. First, the British blockade slowly starved Germany of food, raw materials and morale. Second, the German U-boat campaign of 1917 came close to forcing Britain out of the war by starvation but instead drew the United States in — American protests against unrestricted submarine warfare combined with the Zimmermann Telegram to bring the USA into the war in April 1917. Third, the convoy system from May 1917 contained the U-boat threat and ensured the safe arrival of the American Expeditionary Force in 1918. The war was won partly on the sea lanes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on the U-boat campaign, the highest band rewards three or four linked events, not a chronology of dates. Use connectives such as ‘this triggered’, ‘as a result’, ‘which forced’. Specific named detail wins marks: 1 February 1917 unrestricted submarine warfare; April 1917 worst month at 881,000 tons; first convoy from Gibraltar in May 1917; convoy losses then halved. Avoid the first-person voice or any ‘diary entry’ framing — AQA examiner reports flag this as a recurring issue that prevents top marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jutland (31 May–1 June 1916) was a tactical draw but a strategic British win — the German High Seas Fleet retreated to port and the British blockade tightened.
  • Germany’s gamble on unrestricted submarine warfare from 1 February 1917 nearly starved Britain (881,000 tons sunk in April 1917) but pulled the USA into the war by April.
  • The convoy system, introduced from May 1917, halved shipping losses and ensured the safe arrival of American troops in 1918, sealing the fate of the U-boat campaign.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a private letter by Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty to his wife, written aboard HMS Lion on the night of 31 May 1916, drawn from the Beatty Papers held at the National Maritime Museum.
‘There is something wrong with our bloody ships today. Three battlecruisers gone in an afternoon — magazines unprotected, signalling slow, the German gunnery sharper than I had supposed. Yet we have driven Scheer back to his base and there he will stay.’

Using Source A, identify two features of the Battle of Jutland.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct features drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant features from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear feature; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific features.

Indicative content:
• Three British battlecruisers were lost during the action (‘three battlecruisers gone in an afternoon’).
• British ships had design weaknesses, especially unprotected magazines (‘magazines unprotected’).
• German gunnery was more accurate than expected (‘the German gunnery sharper than I had supposed’).
• The strategic outcome was that the German fleet retreated to base (‘we have driven Scheer back to his base’).

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the German U-boat campaign developed from the first declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1915 to the introduction of the convoy system in May 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Feb 1915 declaration, Lusitania 7 May 1915, 1 Feb 1917 resumption, April 1917 tonnage, first convoy May 1917); reaches the convoy system through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• February 1915: Germany declared the first unrestricted submarine warfare campaign in the waters around Britain.
• 7 May 1915: U-20 sank the RMS Lusitania off Ireland, killing 1,198 including 128 Americans; US protests forced Germany to suspend unrestricted attacks in late 1915.
• 1 February 1917: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, calculating six months of attacks could starve Britain into peace before the USA could intervene.
• March 1917: Zimmermann Telegram became public, contributing to US declaration of war on 6 April 1917.
• April 1917: 881,000 tons of British merchant shipping sunk — Britain estimated to have around six weeks of food remaining.
• May 1917: experimental convoy from Gibraltar to Britain lost no ships, prompting a system-wide shift to convoying that halved monthly losses by the end of 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Admiral Sir John Jellicoe to the British War Cabinet on 27 June 1917, drawn from Admiralty records.
‘The losses in merchant shipping have reached a level beyond what our island can sustain. Without an immediate change in tactics — the gathering of merchantmen into convoys under naval escort — we shall be defeated by starvation before the year is out. The Admiralty’s reluctance to proceed must yield to necessity.’

Source C: An extract from a German Admiralty staff paper of August 1917, drawn from German Federal Archives.
‘The British system of convoying has reduced our targets to a needle in a vastly enlarged haystack. To attack we must first find a convoy and then survive the escort. Monthly tonnage destroyed has fallen by more than a third since May. The promise of a six-month decision has not been kept.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the convoy system in 1917. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a senior officer urging the Cabinet to back convoying. Provenance: a memorandum from the First Sea Lord to the War Cabinet, well-placed to know the operational picture but written to overcome internal Admiralty resistance. Own knowledge: April 1917 losses of 881,000 tons; first experimental convoy from Gibraltar in May 1917 lost no ships.
Source C — Content: confirms the convoy system was working from the German side. Provenance: a German Admiralty staff paper, well-placed to assess U-boat performance, written in August 1917 within Germany’s own naval bureaucracy and unlikely to overstate British success. Own knowledge: total Allied losses ultimately around 5,000 ships across the war, but monthly figures halved by late 1917; the U-boats were no longer a strategic threat by 1918.
Judgement: B is useful for the British policy debate; C is highly useful as independent confirmation that convoying defeated the campaign. Together they illuminate both why the system was adopted and how it worked.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from Admiral Reinhard Scheer’s after-action report to the Kaiser, dated 4 June 1916.
‘The Imperial Navy met the British Grand Fleet at Jutland and inflicted heavier losses than it suffered. Yet the strategic situation is unchanged. The English remain in command of the North Sea, the blockade continues, and our heavy units cannot risk a second engagement of this size.’

Source E: An extract from a 1918 article in The Times of London, looking back on the war at sea.
‘Jutland was no Trafalgar. The Grand Fleet did not destroy its enemy. Yet by holding the seas it has slowly drained Germany of food, fuel and faith. The blockade, not the battle, has done the work.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The British naval blockade was the most important factor in defeating Germany.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Both sources point to the blockade as a slow but decisive lever — Source D acknowledges the strategic failure to break it; Source E credits it directly.
• Roughly 750,000 German civilians died from blockade-related causes; the ‘Turnip Winter’ of 1916–17 broke morale; the Kiel mutiny of October 1918 began among hungry sailors.
• Jutland’s strategic outcome made the blockade workable by keeping the High Seas Fleet in port.
Challenging the claim:
• Other factors mattered as much: US entry to the war (April 1917) and the arrival of the AEF in 1918; the failure of the Spring Offensive (March–July 1918); the Hundred Days; tactical/operational learning by the BEF.
• The blockade was a slow burn, not a knockout — Germany was still capable of major offensives in March 1918.
• Internal political collapse in 1918 had multiple causes including military defeat and the Bolshevik example, not only food shortage.
Provenance points: Scheer (Source D) writes officially to defend his command and acknowledge strategic limits; The Times (Source E) writes for a public audience after victory, with a journalist’s interpretive framing.
Judgement: the blockade was a major factor and arguably the slowest-acting cause of German defeat; it is a stronger candidate for ‘most important’ in the long run, but combined with US entry and 1918 military reverses rather than alone.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of US Ambassador to Britain Walter Hines Page, written on 3 February 1917 and held at the US Library of Congress.
‘The Germans have today declared their submarines will sink without warning every ship found in the war zone. The President called me from Washington this morning — the long American patience is at an end. American honour, American shipping and American lives can be threatened no longer.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the impact of unrestricted submarine warfare on US policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: pinpoints the reaction of the US ambassador and the President’s tone on the day after the German declaration — useful for tracking the immediate American response.
• Content: shows that loss of US patience was framed in terms of honour, shipping and lives — three threads consistent with Wilson’s subsequent April 1917 war message.
• Provenance: a contemporaneous diary by the senior US diplomat in London, who spoke directly to Wilson, well-placed to record the President’s tone in real time.
• Own knowledge: matches the chronology — Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, the USA broke off diplomatic relations on 3 February, and declared war on 6 April 1917.
• Limitation: the diary is a single observer’s recollection of one phone call — useful but not a full record of US Cabinet discussion.

lessons.title: Russia Out, America In: 1917
lessons.description: Russia's exit at Brest-Litovsk and America's entry in April 1917 — the two great turning points.
lessons.content_html:
The Two Turning Points of 1917

By spring 1917 the war had reached its third winter with no decisive result. Two events that year transformed it. Russia, ground down by huge losses and food shortages, would leave the war altogether by spring 1918. The United States, finally pushed past its tradition of neutrality, would enter the war in April 1917. Both events promised major shifts in manpower — in opposite directions. Germany would gain a free hand in the east; the Allies would eventually gain a vast new pool of soldiers from across the Atlantic.

Key Fact

The United States declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917, triggered by unrestricted submarine warfare from 1 February 1917 and the publication of the Zimmermann Telegram in March 1917. Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918, ending the Eastern Front and freeing around 50 German divisions to move west.

Russia’s Long Collapse

Russia entered the war as a great power and left it as a country in revolution. The huge losses of 1914–16 (around five million casualties), food shortages in the cities, the Tsar’s decision to take personal command of the army in 1915, and the chaotic influence of the mystic Rasputin at home all combined to discredit the Tsarist regime. In late February 1917 (early March in the Western calendar) bread riots in Petrograd grew into a revolution. Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March 1917. A new Provisional Government took over.

The Provisional Government made a fatal decision: continue the war. Its summer 1917 offensive collapsed within weeks. Soldiers began to vote with their feet, deserting in tens of thousands. Germany helped the process: in April 1917 the German government provided the Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin with a sealed train to return from Swiss exile to Petrograd. His promise of ‘Peace, Land and Bread’ gained traction precisely because the Provisional Government refused to make peace.

Lenin’s Bolsheviks seized power on 7 November 1917 (October in the Russian calendar) and immediately opened peace talks. The German terms were ferocious. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, stripped Russia of Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Ukraine and other territories — about a third of its population, half of its industry and almost all its coal. Germany now had a free hand to move troops west. By March 1918 around 50 German divisions had transferred from the Eastern to the Western Front, and Ludendorff was ready to use them.

America’s Long Patience

President Woodrow Wilson had run for re-election in 1916 on the slogan ‘He kept us out of war.’ The United States had a long tradition of avoiding European conflicts, a strong German-American minority, and an economy doing well from selling food and munitions to both sides — though much more to the Allies. Wilson’s position became impossible across the early months of 1917 because of two German decisions.

First, Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, expecting Britain could be starved out in six months. American protests had ended the first U-boat campaign in 1915 after the sinking of the Lusitania (7 May 1915, 1,198 dead including 128 Americans). Wilson immediately broke off diplomatic relations on 3 February 1917. Second, in mid-January 1917 British naval intelligence intercepted and decoded the Zimmermann Telegram, in which the German Foreign Minister proposed an alliance with Mexico against the United States, offering Texas, New Mexico and Arizona as a reward. The British made the telegram public on 1 March 1917. American opinion swung sharply behind war.

Key Fact

Wilson asked Congress to declare war on 2 April 1917 with the words ‘the world must be made safe for democracy’. Congress voted to declare war on 6 April 1917. The first American Expeditionary Force divisions arrived in France in June 1917, but it took until summer 1918 for them to deploy in mass strength — by the armistice in November 1918, around two million American troops were in France.

The Lusitania Misconception

A common student error is to claim the USA ‘joined because of the Lusitania’. The Lusitania sank in May 1915, almost two years before American entry. The sinking generated outrage and forced Germany to suspend unrestricted submarine warfare for over a year, but did not trigger US entry on its own. The actual triggers in 1917 were a combination: the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram revelation on 1 March 1917, against a background of growing economic ties to the Allies and Wilson’s shift towards intervention. Examiner reports flag this misconception every year.

The two turning points worked against each other in time. Russia’s exit gave Germany an immediate manpower advantage from late 1917 into spring 1918 — this was the gap Ludendorff used to launch his Spring Offensive in March 1918, attempting to win the war before American troops arrived in mass. The American Expeditionary Force, by contrast, took time to mobilise, equip, train and ship across the Atlantic. The race against time defined 1918 strategy on both sides. Germany had to win quickly; the Allies had to hold long enough for the Americans to arrive in numbers.

Significance

The 1917 turning points reshaped the war in opposite directions. The fall of the Tsarist regime, the Bolshevik seizure of power and Brest-Litovsk gave Germany its last realistic chance of victory through manpower transfer and a sharper strategic focus. Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram cost Germany America’s neutrality and brought 4.7 million eventual American servicemen into the war on the Allied side. The mismatch in timing — German gains immediate, American gains slow — explains both the German Spring Offensive of March 1918 and its eventual collapse: Germany had only the months between the Russian collapse and the full American deployment to win the war, and could not.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on 1917, examiner reports stress that top-band answers reach a sustained judgement on the named factor versus alternatives. If the question names ‘unrestricted submarine warfare’, weigh it against the Zimmermann Telegram, growing economic ties to the Allies, and Wilson’s shift towards intervention. Use both sources as launchpads, not just description, and bring in precise contextual detail (1 February 1917 declaration, 1 March 1917 publication of telegram, 6 April 1917 vote). Avoid the common Lusitania misconception — the sinking of May 1915 did not directly trigger 1917 US entry.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Russia’s collapse (February and October revolutions of 1917) and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918) ended the Eastern Front and freed around 50 German divisions to move west.
  • The USA declared war on 6 April 1917, triggered by unrestricted submarine warfare (1 February) and the Zimmermann Telegram (1 March), not the 1915 sinking of the Lusitania.
  • The mismatch in timing — German manpower gains immediate, American gains slow — defined 1918 strategy and made the German Spring Offensive a desperate race against the clock.

Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• German actions amount to war already (‘nothing less than war against the government and people of the United States’).
• Unrestricted submarine warfare has sunk neutral as well as Allied shipping (‘vessels of every kind, of every sort and every flag…ruthlessly sent to the bottom’).
• American honour and lives have been threatened (the targeting ‘without warning’).
• A wider democratic mission is invoked (‘the world must be made safe for democracy’).

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Admiral Henning von Holtzendorff, Chief of the German Admiralty Staff, sent to the Kaiser on 22 December 1916, urging the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare. Drawn from German Federal Archives.
‘I do not hesitate to assert that, as the situation now stands, we can force England to make peace within five months by means of an unrestricted submarine campaign. The risk of an American declaration of war is one that we must accept; even if America enters the war, our submarines will starve England out before the new enemy can effectively fight.’

Source C: An extract from a confidential British Cabinet briefing on US opinion, January 1918, drawn from Cabinet Office records.
‘The Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917, made public in our papers in March, transformed American sentiment more decisively than two years of submarine outrages. The proposal to dismember the United States in alliance with Mexico spoke directly to ordinary Americans about the German threat to the homeland.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why the United States entered the war in 1917. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: lays out the German calculation that the U-boat campaign could starve Britain out before America could effectively intervene. Provenance: a memorandum from the Chief of the Admiralty Staff to the Kaiser, written to persuade and likely to overstate certainty. Own knowledge: unrestricted submarine warfare resumed 1 February 1917; Wilson broke relations 3 February; Congress voted to declare war 6 April 1917; April 1917 was the worst month for British shipping (881,000 tons sunk).
Source C — Content: argues that the Zimmermann Telegram, not just submarine warfare, transformed American sentiment. Provenance: a British Cabinet briefing in January 1918, written by officials with access to the British intelligence which had decoded the telegram; well-placed but partial — Britain had a strong interest in framing US entry as a moral response to German conduct. Own knowledge: telegram intercepted mid-January 1917, published 1 March 1917; combined with the resumption of submarine warfare to push Wilson to war.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German thinking but partial as it overstated success and dismissed US weight; C is useful for understanding American public opinion but written from a self-interested British perspective. Together they show why both German decisions were needed to bring the USA in.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the events that led the United States from neutrality at the start of 1917 to a declaration of war in April 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (1 Feb resumption of U-boat war, 3 Feb diplomatic break, mid-Jan interception of Zimmermann Telegram, 1 March publication, 2 April Wilson speech, 6 April vote); reaches the declaration through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1 February 1917: Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare, calculating Britain could be starved out in six months.
• 3 February 1917: Wilson broke off diplomatic relations with Germany.
• Mid-January 1917: British naval intelligence intercepted and decoded the Zimmermann Telegram proposing a German–Mexican alliance against the USA.
• 1 March 1917: Britain made the Zimmermann Telegram public, swinging American opinion sharply.
• March–April 1917: U-boats sank several US-flagged vessels including the Vigilancia and Healdton.
• 2 April 1917: Wilson asked Congress to declare war (‘the world must be made safe for democracy’).
• 6 April 1917: Congress voted to declare war on Germany; first American Expeditionary Force units reached France in June 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from a private letter by German General Erich Ludendorff to a colleague, dated April 1918 and held in the German Federal Military Archives.
‘With the east closed by Brest-Litovsk we have moved fifty divisions to France. The opportunity exists now and only now: before the Americans arrive in their millions. Our offensive must succeed in the next three months or it will not succeed at all.’

Source E: An extract from a 1929 history of the war by British historian Basil Liddell Hart.
‘The events of 1917 were two interlocked turning points moving in opposite directions. Russia’s collapse gave Germany its only window for victory. America’s entry guaranteed the window would close. The 1918 campaigns were the consequences of that race.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘US entry in April 1917 was the most important turning point of the war.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source E credits American entry with closing the window for German victory.
• By the armistice ~2 million American troops were in France; eventually 4.7 million Americans served.
• American intervention transformed Allied morale, finance and grand strategy.
• Convoying — protected by US destroyer cooperation — defeated the U-boat campaign that nearly forced Britain out of the war.
Challenging the claim:
• Source D shows German strategy was driven by the Russian collapse — Brest-Litovsk freed 50 divisions and gave Germany its only realistic chance to win in early 1918.
• Other strong candidates include the failure of the Spring Offensive (March–July 1918), the Hundred Days, the British naval blockade and German internal collapse.
• American troops were not decisive in numbers until summer 1918 — for most of 1917 the entry had little immediate military weight.
Provenance points: Ludendorff (Source D) writes from the German operational viewpoint and frames events to justify his Spring Offensive gamble; Liddell Hart (Source E) writes a decade later within a critical interwar tradition.
Judgement: US entry was a major turning point but its significance lay in combination with Russian collapse — the two interlocking events of 1917 reshaped 1918, with neither sufficient on its own.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a despatch by British ambassador to Russia Sir George Buchanan to the Foreign Office, dated 16 March 1917 and held in the National Archives.
‘The Tsar abdicated yesterday. The army is no longer reliable; the Petrograd garrison sided with the rioters. A Provisional Government has been formed which intends to continue the war. I would advise that this intention rests on a fragile base of public support.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the Russian Revolution of 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: confirms the date of the abdication (15 March 1917) and that the Petrograd garrison had joined the protests — useful for tracking the army’s defection from the regime.
• Content: records the Provisional Government’s decision to continue the war, with the ambassador’s prediction that public support was fragile — a foreshadowing of the later July offensive collapse and Bolshevik takeover.
• Provenance: a contemporaneous despatch from the senior British diplomat in Petrograd; well-placed and writing for an internal audience, less likely to perform than a public statement.
• Own knowledge: matches the chronology — the Provisional Government’s summer 1917 offensive collapsed, Lenin returned in April 1917 in the German sealed train, and Bolsheviks seized power on 7 November 1917.
• Limitation: a single despatch reflects an outsider’s reading; Buchanan was sympathetic to the Provisional Government and may have understated revolutionary momentum.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Russia moved from continued participation in the war in March 1917 to the signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918.
practice_questions.marks:

Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.

Indicative content:
• 15 March 1917: Tsar Nicholas II abdicated after Petrograd bread riots; a Provisional Government took power and chose to continue the war.
• April 1917: Germany allowed Lenin a sealed train back to Petrograd, calculating that Bolshevik agitation would weaken Russian war commitment.
• Summer 1917: Provisional Government’s ‘Kerensky Offensive’ collapsed within weeks; tens of thousands of soldiers deserted.
• 7 November 1917: Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd (October by Russian calendar); immediate offer of peace talks to Germany.
• December 1917: armistice on the Eastern Front opened the way to formal negotiations.
• 3 March 1918: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk signed; Russia surrendered Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Ukraine and other territories — about a third of its population. Around 50 German divisions began transferring west for the Spring Offensive.

lessons.title: Spring Offensive, Hundred Days and Armistice
lessons.description: Ludendorff's Spring Offensive, the Hundred Days and the Kaiser's abdication — how the war ended.
lessons.content_html:
A Race Against Time

By spring 1918 Germany’s strategic position was paradoxical. On the surface it had never looked stronger. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 had ended the Eastern Front and freed around 50 divisions for the Western Front. The U-boat campaign had not yet been decisively beaten. Below the surface things were grim. The British naval blockade had reduced the home front to near-starvation. Industrial output was falling. The American Expeditionary Force was building rapidly in France — around 250,000 American soldiers were arriving every month by mid-1918. Ludendorff knew that if he did not win the war by summer, he would not win it at all.

Key Fact

Operation Michael, the first phase of the German Spring Offensive, opened on 21 March 1918 with the largest artillery barrage of the war — 6,600 guns fired over a million shells in five hours. Using stormtrooper tactics, German troops advanced up to 65 kilometres in a week — the largest gain by either side since 1914.

The Spring Offensive Runs Out of Steam

Ludendorff launched five separate offensives between March and July 1918: Michael (Somme), Georgette (Lys), Blücher (Aisne), Gneisenau (Matz) and Friedensturm (Marne). The opening blows shocked the British Fifth Army into the longest retreat of the war. By April British commanders were so worried Haig issued the famous ‘backs to the wall’ order. In response, on 26 March 1918 the Allies appointed French general Marshal Ferdinand Foch as Generalissimo — a single allied commander coordinating all forces. Allied unity, scrambled into being by crisis, was Germany’s most important new enemy.

Then the offensive began to fail. The reasons were structural. Stormtrooper tactics had no follow-through — once the lead infiltrators ran ahead of their supplies, they could not be reinforced. The advance overran territory but missed strategic objectives like the railway hub at Amiens. German losses were heavy: about a million casualties between March and July, including the elite stormtrooper divisions Ludendorff could not replace. By July, Germany had simply burned through its strategic reserve. The Friedensturm offensive on the Marne was met by a coordinated French and American counter-attack on 18 July 1918, marking the end of the German initiative.

Stormtroopers carried light weapons (sub-machine guns, grenades, flamethrowers) and were trained to flow around enemy strongpoints rather than attack them head-on. The tactics were brilliant at tactical breakthrough — they gave Germany the largest single-day gains of the war. But infiltration outran logistics. The German army still moved supplies, reserves and artillery by horse and foot, while the British and French had pre-prepared rail-supplied defensive zones. Each offensive opened spectacularly, then ran out of steam in days. Ludendorff also failed to choose strategic objectives consistently: Michael advanced into open country instead of seizing Amiens. Tactical brilliance without strategic focus produced gains that could not be held.

The Hundred Days

On 8 August 1918 the Allies launched the counter-offensive that became known as the Hundred Days. The opening attack at Amiens combined every tool the BEF had developed: 552 tanks, predicted artillery fire (no preliminary bombardment to give warning), 800 aircraft, sound-ranging to silence German guns, infantry trained in platoon tactics. The German army broke. Ludendorff called it ‘the black day of the German army’. Eight miles were taken in a day.

The Hundred Days were not one battle but a sustained advance of carefully prepared Allied operations — Amiens, the Hindenburg Line breakthrough at the Canal du Nord (27 September), the Battle of St Quentin Canal (29 September), and the Battle of the Sambre on 4 November. The combination was devastating: combined-arms attacks each rotated along the front so no single sector took permanent strain, supported by overwhelming American manpower (over a million troops in the line by autumn 1918) and dwindling German reserves. The combined-arms approach forged through 1915–17 was now winning the war.

Key Fact

Five interlocking factors broke Germany in 1918: failed Spring Offensive (manpower exhaustion); American manpower (~250,000/month arriving); the Allied combined-arms learning curve; the British naval blockade; and German internal collapse (Kiel mutiny, abdication). No single factor was sufficient on its own.

Internal Collapse

By autumn 1918 the German home front was breaking. The blockade had killed roughly 750,000 civilians and pushed urban populations to the edge. Germany’s allies collapsed in succession — Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September 1918, the Ottoman Empire on 30 October, Austria-Hungary on 3 November. On 28 October the German High Seas Fleet was ordered to make a final suicidal sortie against the Royal Navy; sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than obey. The mutiny spread inland in days. Workers’ councils took control in Munich and other cities.

Ludendorff resigned on 27 October 1918. Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November 1918, fleeing to the Netherlands. A new German republican government, hastily declared, sent representatives to a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne, where French Marshal Foch presented terms. The armistice was signed at 5am on 11 November 1918 and took effect at 11am that morning — ending the fighting at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month.

In the Hundred Days the BEF inflicted defeats on the German army that few other forces achieved in the entire war. Roughly 188,000 German prisoners were taken between August and November 1918 by British and Empire troops alone. Foch’s strategic coordination as Allied Generalissimo from late March 1918 ensured the Allies attacked Germany at multiple points simultaneously, never letting reserves rest. Revisionist historians (Sheffield, Simkins, Todman) argue these victories should weigh against the ‘butcher and bungler’ verdicts that dominate popular memory. The most balanced view: Haig and Foch presided over a force that had learned its trade through hard losses and finished the war as the most effective fighting army in the world.

Significance

November 1918 ended fifty-one months of fighting that had killed around 9 million soldiers and shaped the rest of the twentieth century. The German army had been beaten on the battlefield, but no Allied soldier had set foot on German soil — a fact that allowed the post-war ‘stab-in-the-back’ myth to take hold. The combination of factors that produced the armistice cuts directly across single-cause explanations. America’s manpower mattered, but only because it arrived in time and the Allies held long enough. The blockade mattered, but only because Jutland kept the High Seas Fleet bottled up. Generalship mattered, but only with the combined-arms toolkit forged through 1915–17. Internal German collapse mattered, but it was triggered by military defeat in the field. Top-band essays weigh these factors together, with judgement and evidence, rather than picking one alone.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on why Germany lost in 1918, AQA examiner reports flag single-cause answers (‘America joined’ or ‘the blockade’) as a recurring weakness. Top-band responses weigh the named factor against alternatives: failed Spring Offensive, US manpower (~250,000/month), Allied combined-arms (Amiens 8 August), the blockade (~750,000 German civilian deaths), internal collapse (Kiel mutiny, Kaiser’s abdication 9 November). Use precise figures and dates. Reach a substantiated overall judgement, not a fence-sitting summary.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ludendorff’s Spring Offensive (21 March–mid-July 1918) used stormtrooper tactics for the largest gains since 1914 but burned through Germany’s reserves; Foch’s appointment as Allied Generalissimo on 26 March produced unified Allied command.
  • The Hundred Days (8 August–11 November 1918) combined combined-arms tactics, mass tanks, US manpower and dwindling German reserves into a sustained Allied advance; Amiens was Ludendorff’s ‘black day’.
  • The armistice (11am, 11 November 1918) followed military defeat plus internal collapse: blockade-driven starvation, the Kiel mutiny (28 October), the Kaiser’s abdication (9 November) — no single factor explains the German defeat.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a German army diary entry by Captain Rudolf Binding, written near the Somme on 28 March 1918, drawn from his published memoir A Fatalist at War (1929).
‘We have advanced further in seven days than the Allies advanced in the whole of 1916. The British defences crumbled before our barrage and our infantry. Yet our supplies cannot keep pace with our men, and the men themselves are tired beyond what fresh divisions can fix. The advance has begun to outrun what we can hold.’

Using Source A, identify two features of the German Spring Offensive in March 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct features drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant features from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear feature; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific features.

Indicative content:
• The Spring Offensive achieved very rapid initial advances (‘further in seven days than the Allies advanced in the whole of 1916’).
• The British defences collapsed under bombardment and infantry attack (‘the British defences crumbled before our barrage and our infantry’).
• Logistics could not keep pace with the advance (‘our supplies cannot keep pace with our men’).
• German troops were exhausted and could not be replaced (‘the men themselves are tired beyond what fresh divisions can fix’).

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the German Spring Offensive developed between its opening on 21 March 1918 and the Allied counter-attack on the Marne on 18 July 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Operation Michael 21 March, Foch as Generalissimo 26 March, Haig ‘backs to the wall’, the five offensives, Marne 18 July); reaches the close through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 21 March 1918: Operation Michael opened with 6,600 guns firing over a million shells in five hours; stormtrooper tactics broke the British Fifth Army.
• 26 March 1918: Marshal Foch appointed Allied Generalissimo, coordinating all Allied forces — a direct response to the breakthrough.
• 11 April 1918: Haig issued his ‘backs to the wall’ order during Operation Georgette.
• April–June 1918: further offensives (Blücher, Gneisenau) reached the Marne and were within 50 miles of Paris but missed strategic objectives.
• Through July: stormtrooper logistics broke down; about a million German casualties from March to July, including elite divisions Ludendorff could not replace.
• 18 July 1918: French and American counter-attack at the Marne (the Friedensturm offensive) ended the German initiative for good.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by General Erich Ludendorff to Field Marshal von Hindenburg, dated 9 August 1918 and held in the German Federal Military Archives.
‘Yesterday — the eighth of August — was the black day of the German army. The morale of certain divisions on the Amiens front broke under the combined assault of tanks, aircraft and an artillery barrage we had not anticipated. We can no longer count on victory. Defensive war has become our only option.’

Source C: An extract from the British official despatch on the Battle of Amiens, written by Field Marshal Haig and forwarded to the War Cabinet on 12 August 1918.
‘On 8 August our Fourth Army, supported by 552 tanks and 800 aircraft, attacked along an eleven-mile front. The advance reached eight miles by nightfall. Some 13,000 prisoners and 200 guns were taken. The German army did not stand and fight in the manner we had grown to expect.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Battle of Amiens (8 August 1918). Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Ludendorff’s blunt admission that 8 August broke the German army. Provenance: an internal memo to his superior; written candidly to alert command, not to perform. Own knowledge: Amiens combined 552 tanks, 800 aircraft, predicted fire and combined-arms infantry — the BEF’s mature toolkit.
Source C — Content: Haig’s detailed numbers (552 tanks, 800 aircraft, 13,000 prisoners, 200 guns, eight miles in a day) confirm the scale and method. Provenance: an official despatch by the British commander to the War Cabinet, well-placed but partly intended to defend his command’s record. Own knowledge: 8 August opened the Hundred Days; ~188,000 German prisoners were taken by British and Empire troops between August and November 1918.
Judgement: Both highly useful. B is unusually candid for a senior German commander, providing rare insight into German morale; C is detailed and procedural, with the limit that Haig had reasons to highlight British achievement. Together they build a strong picture of the battle’s tactical and psychological impact.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from a 1925 article in The Round Table magazine, summarising British public opinion on why Germany lost the war.
‘The blockade did the work. Year by year it ground down German strength until the home front broke. The army was beaten on the field, but only because the country behind it had been starved into despair.’

Source E: An extract from a 1991 article by historian Gary Sheffield in History Today.
‘In the Hundred Days the British Expeditionary Force inflicted decisive defeats on the German army using combined-arms tactics, fresh American manpower, mass tanks and predicted artillery fire. The military victory of August–November 1918 was the proximate cause of the armistice; the blockade and internal collapse were necessary contributing factors but not, by themselves, sufficient.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘Germany lost the war because of internal collapse on the home front, not military defeat.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D credits the blockade as the ultimate cause; ~750,000 German civilians died from blockade-related malnutrition and disease.
• ‘Turnip Winter’ 1916–17, Kiel naval mutiny on 28 October 1918, workers’ councils in cities, Kaiser’s abdication 9 November.
• Bulgaria, Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian collapses (29 Sept, 30 Oct, 3 Nov 1918) preceded armistice.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E emphasises the military victory of the Hundred Days as the proximate cause — Amiens (Ludendorff’s ‘black day’), Hindenburg Line breakthrough, ~188,000 German prisoners to BEF alone.
• Failed Spring Offensive (March–July 1918): million casualties; loss of elite stormtrooper divisions; logistics that could not be replaced.
• American manpower (~250,000/month) in time to matter.
• Internal collapse was triggered by military defeat — the Kiel mutiny followed orders for a final suicidal sortie under Allied pressure.
Provenance points: Source D from 1925 fits a public framing that suited British self-image (winning by economic strength rather than carnage); Source E sits within a peer-reviewed academic tradition with later access to records.
Judgement: ‘not military defeat’ overstates the case. The blockade and internal collapse were necessary; military defeat in the Hundred Days was the trigger. The combination won the war, with military victory as the proximate cause.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Sir Maurice Hankey, secretary to the British War Cabinet, recording events in early November 1918. Held in the Hankey Papers at Churchill College, Cambridge.
‘News from Kiel: sailors mutinied rather than put to sea against the Royal Navy. Workers’ councils now reported in Munich. The Kaiser’s position is untenable. A republican government will form within days, and we shall meet German envoys in Foch’s railway carriage at Compiègne. The eleventh hour approaches.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the German collapse in November 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: confirms key elements of the collapse — Kiel mutiny against orders for a final naval sortie, workers’ councils in Munich — useful corroboration of the home-front breakdown.
• Content: notes the unsustainability of the Kaiser’s position and the imminent armistice negotiations at Compiègne; useful evidence of how British officials read the speed of events.
• Provenance: a contemporaneous diary by the Cabinet secretary, well-placed and writing internally; less performative than a published memoir.
• Own knowledge: matches the chronology — the Kiel mutiny began 28 October 1918, Kaiser abdicated 9 November 1918, armistice signed 5am 11 November and took effect at 11am.
• Limitation: a single observer’s diary captures the British view of German collapse, not the German experience itself; the entry compresses several developments into a single, retrospective tone.

Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.

• 8 August 1918: Battle of Amiens; combined-arms attack with 552 tanks, 800 aircraft, predicted fire and infantry took eight miles in a day. Ludendorff called it ‘the black day of the German army’.
